- His death-blow struck him, there in the ranks -- There in the ranks, with his face to the foe: Did his dying lips utter curses or thanlo? No one will knew.
R A S.

Still he marched on, he with the rest— Still he marched on, with his face to the foe, To the day's bitter business sternly, _addrest: Dead—did they know? When the day was over, the fierce fight done, His cheeks were red with the sunset's glow, And they crowned hica there with their laurels won: Dead—did he know?. Laurels or roses, a one to lifenow— What to a dead man is glory or glow ? Base wreaths tor love, or a crown on his brow : Dead—does he know? And yet you will see him march on with the rest— No man of them all makes a goodlier show— In the thick of the tumult jostled and prest : Dead—would you know?
WELLS THAT NEVER FREEZE.

-az Nature's wells are deep below, Deep below the line of frost and snow; They are clear and sparkling, cool and sweet, Clear and sparkling underneath our feet, Cool through all the summer's heat, e Free through winter's frost and snOw. , For the wells that Nature digs Are below the line of change,
tongue- No)•

Deer, deep below. - - Nature's wells are never dry When the August sun is blazing high, They are deep and cool, they are cool and iiegv, i And n rocky cisterns moisture keep For the finest seeds that sleep, For the roots of mighty trees, For the thirsty lips that know Nature's wells are far below The line of change. My life's wells lie far below, Far below the line of frost and snow; Safely hid within my home they lie, Deep and still and sweet beneath Love's sky. Frost and heat and wind pass by; Life has drought and frost outside, But the household wells still flow Clear and sweet and far below The line of change. For home's wells are never dry, Outside oft the conflict waxes high, And a bitter drought is on the strife, Or a frost ties fast the hopes of life; Then, at home, by side of child anegwife, Are the wells that never fail, Are the household wells that flow Sweet and deep and clear, below The line of change. —Leeds .Ifercury Supplement.

Young ladies, please note. I 4' Yes," said the landlord, pointing to his block of new houses, "they're all full 'cept the one at the end. That's i last, but not leased." "What is wisdom?" asked a teacher of a class of small girls. A bright-eyed little creature arose and answered, "Information of the brain." Louise, who was staying at the sea-side, saw for the first time the white caps on the water, and exclaimed, " 0 mamma, the water has all blossomed out." Music teacher: "You see that note with an open space? That's a whole note. Can you remember that?' Scholar : " Yes'm; &whole note is a note that has-a hole in it." "Poor creatures ! " exclaimed Mrs. Grosgrain, looking at the pictures of nude savage women; "no clothing of any kind! I wonder what the poor things have to talk about?" An English physician says a man can stop a fit of sneezing by crawling downstairs head first. Almost any- thing can be cured in that way if the stairs be _steep enough. . "Well, Sniffles, have you posted the ledger?" • New Clerk, " Yeth, thir, I've pothted the ledger; ieut, lor, thir, it wath too big for the letter-botch, the I had to take it inthicle th poditoffitb." A debating society has been discussing the question, "'ls it worse to think you have reached the top when there is one stair more, than to think there is one stair more when you have reached the top, and bring your foot down so hard that it tingles for four hours?" Lord Palraerston,-at an anniversary of the Romsay Agricultural Association, in presenting to an old woman a money prize of ten shillings for keeping her cottage and garden orderly and neat, said, " We have heard of a virtuous woman being a crown to her husband, but here is one who is worth two crowns !" At the time, some years ago, when light gold was dif- ficult to pass, a gentleman, not liking to attempt to pass a lith: half-sovereign, sent his Irish servant to do so, and OIL return asked him for the change. "Sure, I passed it, yer honour." "You are a clever fellow," said his master. "110 w did you manage it ?" "Oh, faith, sir," said he, "I stuck it between two halfpence at the turn- pike-gate, yer honour, and the fellow never saw it." A gentleman of the Temple received his charwoman's bill made out in the style of spelling and handwriting peculiar to that class; but there was one item of one shilling and sixpence which defied even his practised comprehension—it was for "skewering the stars." After wondering for some time how such a work could ever have been performed. and still more how it should have been executed particularly at his expense, the debtor Isent for Mrs. Pearlash, when the reading turned out to be "for scouring the stairs," "Gentlemen," said the professor to the assembled medical students, "I have often pointed out to you the , remarkable tendency to consumption of those who play ' upon wind instruments. In this case now before us, we have a well-marked development of lung disease; • and I was not surprised to find, on questioning the , patient, that he is a member of a brass band. Now, sir," continued the professor, addressing the consumptive, "will you please tell the gentlemen what instrument you play on?" "I Ways der drum;" said the sick man. % A Pennsylvania girl sued a former lover for breach of ! promise, and produced several of his letters with post- scripts containing promises of marriage, to substantiate ) her claim. The Court, however, threw the letters out, • inasmuch as it was discovered that in the postscripts, when the personal pronoun was necessary, a small "i" I was used, while in the body of the letter it appeared • properly as a capital, showing that the two parts of the i epistle had not been written by the same hand. The / young woman lost her case, and 'will nrobalily learn to [ write properly before she tries that doge again. [ 'NEEDED Discrrtnix.—The duty of self-knowledge and 0 self-culture along some one definite line should be im- pressed on every young person. It is not selfish; on the contrary, it is what makes it possible to be of any real ' ' good to others. For, when any one is doing his own . true work in the best way, he is always benefiting his ' fellow-men, whether he is conscious of it or not. Beyond this, however, it is chiefly through the discipline of this t culture that we come to understand others and to know . how to help them. One who is vigorously bending him- self to his own life-duties is in a far better position to , give intelligent aid to others in their struggles than one [ who, having no purpose, devotes himself to forming or mending those of other people. o Himrs Fon DAILY LlFE.—Thewhole experience of both , men and women is a warfare between the good they ; would do and the evil they would do. When we can we I should sleep over every injury or annoyance. The pillow I is a most excellent councillor, and everyone must have • noticed how differently things look at the time of happen- ing and next day. It is well to remember that very few • people regard words in just the same sense: This is par- ticularly the case with uneducated persons, as very often impertinence is simply ignorance. It is impossible that offences will not come, and men;who go into the market" places of the world are certain—however circumspect their conduct may be—to meet them. If ill-temper is caused by weariness of body, rest and refreshment is the best cure; if by exhausted mental powers, try a change of scene or occupation, or take a walk in the open air. A woman should often drop her sewing to play with her baby, or go into the kitchen She will find by changing her work she will be happier than if she sat hour after hour over some one thing. - A Panora/mita MOUSE.—" We do live in the meanest little hole in the world, mamma," said a young lady mouse. "I really am ashamed of asking my fashionable friends to call." • Well, my dear, I was born in this hole, and it has been the homestead of our family since our remote ancestor came over in a big cheese in the May Flower. But times change, and we must change with them." So to please her daughter the good-natured matron had the hole enlarged and the furniture reno- vated, and by the addition of a few articles of vertu and bric-a-brac it assumed quite a genteel appearance. One day, returning from a ramble, they found an old rat had taken possession. They asked him very civilly to leave their hole. "Your hole." he exclaimed; "don't tell me this is a mouse-hole. It is a rat hole. Look at its size. A cousin of mine died in this neighbourhood lately, and this must be his house, and I will keep it." Moral.— Some people go on enlarging their hooses, their ideas, and their expenses, till at last too much enlarging bursts up everything. We look for them in vain, and find their luxurious dwellings have passed into other hands.— Cassell's Family Magarbie. WHAT EVERY GIRL SHOVED LEARN.—To sew; to cook; to mend; to avoid idleness; to respect old ago- to mind the baby; to darn stockings; to hold her tongue; to keep a house tidy; to be abovegossiping; to make home happy ; to control her temper; to humour a cross man; to take care of the sick; to sweep down cobwebs; to use neither paint nor powder; to see a mouse without screaming; to read some books besides novels; to wear shoes that won't cramp her feet; to wear corks in which she can breathe; to get into a mother-in-law's good graces; to be neat and clean about her own per- son; to live on more healthful diet than pastry and candies ; to be polite to all people at all times and in all places; to distinguish a suit of clothes from the man who wears them; to know how to appreciate a good husband when she gets one; M respect herself that she may know how to win respect from others; w be mis- tress of some branch of industry if she is to depend on her own exertions for a living; to look on a man as a creature with a head and heart, and not as a mere ma- chine to turn out so many pounds a week and keep a woman in all the solid comforts of life and gratify her - whim and caprice. - --

every , Bovallo a FaEsIDIA.N.—As to introducing freshmen, at some colleges the tutor selected a kind of ProxenoS, or introducer and patron general. Such a one was my old friend Newman, while at Wadham, before he became Demi of Magdalen College. Alas, poor Newman! Much fun, wit and merriment died when he departed this life —not an unpleasant life to him—about three years since. Old Dr. Cyril, a very celebrated dean of Christ Church, once remarked that he should not wish to have all reading men; he wanted some idle men, to make diversions and variety for the studious. Just such a man was Newman, and such appeared to have been his special mission. He was a very Yoric in Oxford life. Well, Newman, when no longer a freshman, grew im- patient of the honours of showing, as he said, a set of raw, beardless boys about the premises, and explaining for the twentieth time the etiquette and customs of the place. "So," said he,"! thought at last I was entitled to a little amusement in consideration of my off-time duties and as one who had done the State some service. So, after indoctrinating one, more verdant than usual with strange notions of the exceeding familiarity which existed between the undergraduates and the *Dons,' I left in his room a note in the name of Mr. Vores, a col- lege tutor, to the following effect Dear Sir,—Observ- ing that your rooms form an angle with mine at the corner of the quadrangle, and as I presume we are equally inconvenienced by the necessity of a fire for breakfasts these hot mornings, I write to propose, and to explain a plan I have invented for mutually boiling each other's kettles. The accompanying sketch will best show how easily a rod can pass from your window to mine, made so that the ends can slip in and out of a .groove, to send the kettle on its little travels backwards and forwards by help of a string on your side and on mine. Now I will boil the kettle on Mondays, Wednes- days, and Fridays, if you will render me the same ser- vice on the Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays, and Sun- days.—Yours truly, A. VORES. P.S.—Let me know your shaving hour, that we may arrange matters accord- ingly.' It was only last year that my old friend Whitehead laughed as he related how this simple fellow ' came into Mr. Vores's rooms where a class of fifteen men was deep in Aristotle, and put the tutor to confusion and all the class to the titter by saying :—" Sir, I am come to accept your proposal." "Proposal? About what ?" "About boiling our kettles alternate mornings, and—" " I don't understand you—but—but after Lecture I will speak toyou."—Lotzelon Society. Man is happy in proportion to his freedom from cares, even as the saints of God. The crosses we make for ourselves by anxiety as to the future are not the crosses sent by God To be very iensitive to trifles, and to take important matters easily, is the mark of a strange reversal of feeling. It is a truth worth remembering that this mortal life is given to us solely that we may prepare for life im- mortal. Rest? we shall rest in eternity, Josiah Benson, a manufacturer, took into his office a nephew who, to put it mildly, was rather feeble-minded. One day the nephew came to his uncle and complained of the head clerk, Jones. "Uncle, what do you suppose that clerk Jones has been telling people about me ?" 'I have no idea." "He has been telling everybody that I am a fool." "I will see him about it, and tell him to keep quiet about it. He has no right to expose the secrets of this office." A young woman, who thought she was lqsingVier husband's affection, went to a seventh daughter of a seventh daughter for a love-powder. ,The mystery woman told her—" Get a raw piece of beef, cut flat, about an inch thick. Slice an onion in two, and rub the meat on both sides with it. Put on pepper and salt, andi toast it on each side over a red coal fire. Drop on it three lumps of butter and two sprigs of parsley, and get him to eat it." The young wife did so, and her husband lover her ever after. Swift was everywhere received by the common people with the most profound respect. Upon one occasion he made a ludicrous experiment on the public belief in his authority. A number of persons having assembled around the Deanery to see an eclipse, Swift became tired of their:noise, and commanded the crier to make pro- clamation that the eclipse was put off by coramand of the Dean of St. Patrick's. This extraordinary enuncia- tion was received with great gravity, and was the means of dispersing the assembled gazers. The Empress of Austria was walking incognita near Ischl, when she met two little girls returning from schooL After some conversation and the distribution of some candy, she bade them good night. " Good night, Madame l'lmperatrice," replied the elder child. "What, you know me? Why didn't you say so before?" asked the Empress. "Because, madame," was the re- ply, "I have been taught that in this world one shonkl never know too much. It is reported that the sovereign lady was so impressed by the answer that the clever school-girl will have reason to remember the interview. Tile OMISSION or A CoseasA.—Some years ago the omis- sion of a comma in a letter to the London nines gave a horrible meaning to a sentence. The letter is on the American war, and the writer :says :—" The loge of life will hardly fall short of a quarter of a million; and how many more were better with the dead than doomed to crawl on the mutilated victims of this great national crime." It should have been "than doomed to crawl. on the mutilated victims of this great national crime." The following sentence appearedn a newspaper a short time ago, "The prisoner said the witness was a con,-,, victeethief." This statement :nearly caused the pro- prietors of the newspaper some trouble, and yet the words were correct. When their attention was drawn to the matter, and proper punctuation supplied, the sen- tence had an exactly opposite meaning. "The prisoner, said the witness, was a convicted thief." Dean Ilford says that he saw an announcement of a meeting in con- nection with the "Society for PrOrnaing the Observance. of the Lord's Day which was founded in 1831," giving the notion that the day, not the society, was founded in that year. A comma should have been after*" day," and then the sentence would have been correct. In the Pall Ga:ette recently the Rev. H. R. Haweis called atten- tion:to an awkward misplacement of invertedgcommas in an article by him on the late Duke of Wellington, whereby some words of the late Duke, about Mr. Glad- stone's speeches, are attributed to the Duke's illustrious father.—Alf the Year Round. THE BARBER OF DUNSE.—A clergyman, possessing an uncommon share of wit and humour, had occasion to lodge for the night, in company with some friends, at the inn of a town which, for certain reasons, we shall denominate Dunse. Requiring the services of a barber, he was recommended by the waiter to Walter Dron, who was represented as excellent at cracking a joke:or tel- ling a story. This functionary being forthwith:intro- duced, made such a display of his oral and manual dex- terity as t4eave on the mind as well as the body of his customer a very favourable impressiom'and induce the latter to invite him to sit down to a friendly The mutual familiarity which the circulation of he bottle produced, served to show off the barber in his happiest mood, and the facetious clergyman, amid the :general hilarity, thus addressed him— • Now, Wattie, ,engage to give you a guinea on the following terms: .hat yotl leap backward and forward over your chair for the space of half an hour, leisurely yet regularly, crying out at every leap, Here goes I, 4Vattie Dron, barber of Dunse; but that should you utter anything else during the time, you forfeit the reward." Wattle, though no doubt surprised at the absurdity of the proposal, yet considering how easily he could earn the guinea, and the improbability that such an opportunity would ever again Present itself, agreed to the stipulation. The watch was set, and the barber stripped off his coat. Leaning with one hand on the back of a chair, he commenced leaping over the seat, uniformly repeating, in an exulting tone, the words prescribed. After matters had gone on thus for about five minutes, the clergyman rang the bell, and thus accosted the waiter: "What is the reason, sir, you insult me by sending a mad fellow like that instead of a Proper barber, as you pretended he was ?" Barber (leap- ing) "Here goes I, Wattle Dron, barber of Dunse." Waiter: "Oh! sir, I don't know what is the matter; I never saw him in this way in all my life. Mr. Dron ! Mr, Dron! what do you mean?" Barber: "Here goes I," Sic, Waiter: "Bless me, Mr. Dron,", recollect these are gentlemen; how can you make such a fool of your- self ?" Barber: "Hero goes I," Ste. Landlord (entering in haste): "What in the name of wonder, sir, is all this? I—the fellow's mad—how dare you, sir, insult gentlemen in my house by such conduct?" Barber " Here goes &c. Landlord: "I say, Bob, run for his ;:vife, for this can't be put up with. Gentlemen, the man is evidently deranged, e. in any way and I hope you will not let my house be in- 19Td by this business." Barber:" Here goes !c.- Wife (rushing in) : "Oh I Wattle, Wattle, what 's rals that's come ower ye? Do ye ken your wife ?" Barber: " Here goes I," &lc. Wife (weeping): "Oh, Wattle, if ye care for me, mind yer bairns at bane, and come awa' wi: me." Barber: "Here goes I," &c." " Wat, „ The afflicted wife now clasped her husband round the neck, and hung on him so as to effectuall avert his further progress. Much did poor Wattie struggle to shake MI his loving, yet unwelcome, spouse; but it was "no go "—his galloping was at en end. "Confound you for an idiot," he bitterly exclaimed, "I never could win a guinea so easily in my life." It is only necessary to add that the explanation which immediately followed was much more satisfactory to" mine host" an to the barber's better half, and that the clergyman restored Wattie to his usual good humour by generously reward- ing his exertions with the well-earned guinea. div.head: NER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 14.1885
div.p: NER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 14.1885
COTTAGE GARDENING

RHOBARD.—Werhave frequently read instructions to lift the roots of this and place them in sheds or cellars with the view of hastening the produce, or forcing it as it is termed. Our experience, however, does not justify us in repeating that advice. The last instance of putting it in a cellar that came under our notice was just the reverse of what we are led to expect from those who advocate the system. The roots were put in about Christmas—rather early we admit, but not earlier than is frequently advised. When we were called to inspect it in February or early in March, it had not made a move, whilst that out in the open ground was rapidly develop- ing its crowns and by keeping it covered with litter it was forwarded a fortnight ahead of that left exposed; and as for that in the cellar it did very little good. An- other plan recommended is to place boxes over the crowns, and cover them over with warm manure or any other fermenting material. In cold weather the quan- tity of heating substance required involves much labour in conveying it to the place, as it must be occasionally replenished if it is to be of any service. It is, however, possible to produce much better results with one-fourth of the material if a bed of it two feet thick and a yard wide is made on the surface of the ground in a corner of the garden; for instance, against a wall which will confine the heat on one side at any rate. On this bed spread two inches of soil te lay the roots upon, which should be covered with soil, decayed leaves, or bark, and then place the boxes over the crowns and cover them over with long manure, old sacks or anything else to prevent the heat escaping. Those who reside near tan- yards, or have access to fallen leaves, will have all that is desired to force Rhubarb, so as to have it ready at Christmas if required. Only at that season of the year it will be necessa7 to maintain the heat in the bed by adding a lining to it of any of the fermenting materials named. The roots should not be destroyed after the produce is pulled, but divided into pieces of two or three crowns each. and planted for future use. Some might consider this lifting of the roots a laborious and wasteful process; but it is really not so, for we find that Rhubarb is much finer the second year after planting than that which has remained stationary for a number of years, so that we are amply compensated by the in- creased yield in the open ground, to say nothing of that which is secured by adopting a safe method of forcing. TES Fnorrr GARDEN.—Where the planting of these from various causes has been deferred, there should be no time lost now in attending to it. The dwarf Roses are the most suitable form to plant, and we would not recommend anyone to attempt standards or those worked on the briar in gardens near a town or in smoky districts, as they seldom do well. Roses require a moderate depth of soil, which should be well manured and trenched. It is best to recline the plants at the time of planting, as the wind will not have such power over I them, and the shoots can be secured by hooked wire,' and the other end thrust into tile soil. Ground recently dug or trenched will on most soils be very lumpy, and not at all suitable to place immediately round the roots. Therefore, in making the holes for the plants tinder such circumstances the soil should be placed on one side, or placed in a barrow and moved away, and some more friable soil from some other part of the garden secured to fill up round the roots. Road scrapings and the trimmings of road sides are better still for the purpose. Four inches of soil over the roots will be a sufficient depth, and instead of leaving it loose it should receive moderate pressure from the foot, but any additional soil required need not be trod. After the planting is com- pleted two or three inches of mulching should be placed over the roots of each plant, so as to counteract sudden changes of temperature, as well as atmospheric mois- ture, which act most perniciously on the roots of newly- planted trees. Nearly all kinds of shrubs that are suit- able to dot here and there in the front garden may be planted for some weeks yet. THE Wiarnow.—Tuberous Begonias should receive a slight watering if they have been kept indoors in the windows. • Those buried in ashes will be all right where they are for the present. Fine foliage plants, such as the Indiarubber Plant, Aspidistra Variegate, and the Variegated American Aloe, are in the foremost rank as window or drawing-room plants. The latter requires very little water during the winter; indeed, the soil should always have a dry feel, except of course just after watering. Plants grown for the sake of their foliage should, above all others, be frequently sponged with clean soft water.

PAUL HOLDEN'S VALENTINE.
By PHILIP WEST.
CHAPTER 1. Paul Holden was serving articles to a chemist. Ere half his term was expired, he had come to know that honourable and useful as was the profession yet it was not among the

mysteries of the pestle and mortar that the full circle of energy and talent within him (whether little or much) would be drawn forth, and where he would find the inspira- tion of his life's work. Early in his apprenticship he had stumbled upon a volume of Ruskin's lecture, "The Two Paths." Thence he was beguiled by that wonderful winrd of English dictim into a fairy land—into "pastures new" of ever expanding delight. Ruskin led him to Turner, and that strange and marvellous genius put the light to the sleepiag embers of fancy and awoke dormant chords within ef which he himself had but been vaguely con- scious. . .

One day Paul was intently looking at a print of" Ancient Rome" when he became aware of a new and exquisite sense of discernment into its hidden wealth of imaginative power, into its wondrous witchery of beauty, and he then and there made a vow that he would be artist or nothing—that his pestle and mortar should be the brush and palette—his decoctions from the colour box. This really was the burst- ing of the bud, under genial influences, of Paul's nature. While before he had but seen through a glass darkly—now the scales left his eyes and nature unveiled herself in a fresh and beauteous garb. The fields, the hedges, the wild flowers, the gurgling brooklets, the hush of the glen and the wood, all brought a new message to his soul. And the ever-moving cloud-land now traversed by banks of weird, mists, or hurrying scud, fresh and salt from:the western sea; now compassed by solemn slow-sailing dark masses or by snowy-white cumuli fashioned here into a glittering range of alpine peaks, there into a marching regiment of huge, fantastic balloon-like forms, or to-merrow a wide expanse of purest, heavenliest depths of blue dappered and diapered in tender fleeces of lovliest white, or checkered in a filmy network of pearly gossamer—all still in the hum and peace of a sweet English summer day—this ever-changing world of sky with its mystery, its awe, its gladness, he got to love as we love a daily companion. Thus it was that Paul's soul-birth came to him. To some it comes differently, in a gentle thaw of years, bat to how many thousands of the gold-hunting animal-absorbed creatures around us does it seem never to come at all ! From this period Paul's whole mind and energies were wholly given up to the study of Art. He entered himself as a student at the local School of Art. His imaginative bent made the drudgery of the A.B.C. I all the harder to bear—at times well-nigh unbearable, but he had sense to know that time well spent here was twice ' spent, and so he bravely pegged away. I must hop along, however. Paul had a small patrimony of a few hundred pounds, and upon this, at the end of his term, he went to London resolving this should keep him until he could do some decent work for sale. I will not risk the credence of the reader by telling upon how little he contrived to live. I cannot dwell upon the next three years of his career further than to say that they were stern years of hard study and incessant application, spent at schools and in select claeSes under good masters for the study of the life, Fee. When in due course he felt the growing sense of power and ease in the use of pencil and brush, the canning deftness of lunch and dash responsive to la pretty fancy, or a flesh of feeling, he knew he was a I thousand timea paid for all his self-denial and brave struggle. I must now ask the reader to imagine it St. Valentine's Day juet one year ago. Paul Holden had ever so bog pro- mised himself a treat of a visit to the Reynold's Exhibition at the Grosvenor Gallery, and as he dressed this morning, 14th Feb.. 1884, the tick of his watch seemed to whisper You go to the Grosvenor to-day," Now Peel (though half as'eamed of it) had a sneaking liking for thee old LOW, .iays, so said he "I'll go," .

—Tennyson. Go he did, and early, to get in front of the crowd. He was soon in New Bond-street, passed the turnstile, strode the easy stairs in pairs, was near to the top landing, when his eye ceught an envelope in tint not unlike the carpet. He picked it up ; found it unsealed. Indeed, nearly drop- ping out were two cartes—photographs of a lady. His first impulse was to hand them at once to the attendant, but he could not that face laid hold of bins with an instant fascination, and he could not repress a smile when he felt a gentle flush of warm blood rise high as his temples. The photographs were beautiful specimens of the art, remark- able for the delicacy in their tone and gradation. But the Image—it was so vivid—that it seemed perfectly ready to respond to any number of queries. Paul stowed them in his oreast pocket and walked into gallery No. 1. Only some half dozen visitors were ire the room and there surely was the original of hie miniatures. She was with an elderly lady, doubtless her mother. And now ensued a curious little debate between conscience and feeling not without its touches of c tsuistry. Should he give them to the owner or should he send them by the at- tendant? He would do the latter at once—but they were of no consequence; could be replaced by a score more. She could only be half a crown the worse if she never got them. Anyhow he would not give them up this minute— would feast once more upon them—he roust—could send by post—yes—no—he would not only keep the bits of paste- board, but what is more, by hook or by crook that creature —the original in the flesh should not pass from the sight of his eyes until he saw her enter-the portals of her home or what seemed to be so. The photos—well the course most to his taste was quietly to return them to the photographer, simply saying that he had picked them up, having been dropped. The two ladies had evidently but just arrived, their faces were beaming with interest as they compared the different portraits of the master himself (the first five numbers of the exhibition were all portraits of leeynolds), and Paul was soon convinced that they, like himself, had not came thus early merely as the fashionable thing to do, but for honest pleasure, and from an appreciative and in- telligent inte:est in the collection. How vividly the exhibition lifts one clean over the track of time just 100 years or more ago to the days " when George the third was king." How vividly these living Can- vases bring back the days of dear Horace Walpole when be pasted up his prints at Strawberry Hill and wrote his charming skits and chatty letters upon the fashionable world of his time ; of old Vanecell Gardens when princes of the blood, dukes and duchesses by the dozen frequented that gay resort—when the Thames was alive witu gilded barges and hautboys ; when Fanny Burney played her pretty cheat upon her papa and astonished the world with "Evelma "; the palmy days of the Fleet parson, and the May-fair weddings, of lanthorn, watchmen, and linkboys, now almost as great curiosities a,' a Pompeian urn, to the days when St James's was crowded with courtly ladies and processiens of Sedan chairs. The exhibition is an art treat rich and rare, but the zest and interest are immensely enhanced to him who is familiar with the parts these men and women played in the world of English politics and war art, literature, the drama, fashion, and scandal of a century back, that one is now surrounded by the griandsires and grandanses of maey of the highborn of our time. It is not here my purpose to fellow friend Paul as he slowly paced the galleries. Neither must I dwell upon his delight at the grand modeling of the heads, the masterly drawing and pose, the splendid force and breadth of rich loose colour. Those of my readers who saw that unique assemblage of art treasures will understand the strange effervescence of feeling possessing one in moving amid a crowd or life-endowed portraits painted by a prince in art— and intimate friend to many. Here are Edmund Burke (also his ill-fated son) and Warren Hastings, Garrick and Sheridan, Mrs. Siddone (the great pictwe as:tragic muse), Dr. Johnson, Lady Holland and Mn. Fitzherbert, Angelica Kauffman, A.A., and Bartolozzi, the renowned engraver, that gay beauty, Elizabeth Gunning (one of the three Gun- ning girls), to whose seductive charms the great Duke of Hamilton capitulated, and in hot haete would marry at dead of night, by the Mayfair Parson, the bed curtain hoop for the ring. Here she is quite possessed with as full a share of wits as of beauty. There also is Walpole's, commie- aiOn to Reynolds, his three nieces, all in one picture ; oddly enough they are all three at this very time suffering under love disappointments. They did.not die though, but lived, and all married noblemen. Amid such company—such memories with numerous subject pictures of world wide re- nown—now absorbed In the wonderful expression of a lovely face or captivated with a pair of speaking eyes, Paul was standing before the portrait of bluff-faced old Admiral Kep- pel, when his ear caught a suppressed scream (be assured gentle reader he had not wandered far from your interesting sister). He turned and swift as light he strode a mighty stride, and by a twist of leg caught the falling form on hie right knee and arm. In rising tram a seat she had tripped in her companion's dress—the hard, slippery, treacherous floor carried the slid- ing foot forward, leaving her utterly helpless. She was saved—but Paul? He had managed en one leg to get to a seat. What the deuce was to de with his other he could not tell (and, to speak the truth, neither did he feel to care one pin head) be knew that he fell avikwardly and heavily, and that his leg bad been bents dotibled, and twisted like a willow, and he knew also that if he put one ounce pressure to the duty of- that foe a big groan would escape him. The young lady- was Obtuse with blushing thanks—the elder equally so in eager solicitude as to the nature of his hurt—begged the attendant to fetch the nearest surgeon, and to get a cab; insisted upon knowing Paul's address that her own doctor might attend upon him. To this she would take no denial, and to this Paul was com- pelled to yield, but protested he only needed just now to be taken to a cab, and the doctor would do well enough when at his lodgings, whither he was conveyed with every care and speed.

CHAPTER 111. Oh, there is nothing holier in this life f ours than The first consciousness of love—the first fluttering of its silken wings. —Longfdlow. When Paul described to the doctor his part of the incident at the Grosvenor, he expressed his surprise that his shins were whole, more on account of his own ugly fall than that of his fair burden. Although no bones were cracked, the limb was bad enough in truth. The ankle joint was out— that was soon set right—hut every tendon and ligature, every joint and socket felt as if it were strained, sprained, torn, crushed, and junmed. The pain sometimes was horrible, and he had the pletsant information very emphatically im. parted to him by the doctor that his bedroom must be for several weeks to corns his castle. Every visit of the doctor

brought the most sympathetic words from his new friends, and every week chickens and jams and elegant tastes enough for a month. INow, my reader, I will trouble you no further respecting the accident to Paul's leg. That hapless limb is getting Iquite lively, and is in all conscience lusty enough to take all care of itself, but I will, if you like, inquire in respect of 1 the accident to his heart.
What had become of the pair of photographs? Had be ever once drawn them from the dark hole of his breast
pocket ? asks a fair reader. Nay, don't edge your sarcasm too keenly. Then, did be post then to the phetographer . . . . .

right off -? Bah! His magnanimity took a curious form, viz.,—taking very precious care of them. Ere a fortnight had sped away," these bits of pasteboard," as he was good enough to term them when at the Grosvenor and within six feet of the living and smiling reality—yes, these " bits " were considered of such value as to require and receive a new nest of cleanest, softest tissue about every other day. No* this would, of course, be utterly seedless provided they were never unfolded. The simple fact is evident, it was because they were unfolded so often. Wliere he kept them I cannot swear to, bat I do know he fumbled a good deal about his pi.low cover, and before he had nursed his

leg for three -weeks, one alaksroing thought possessed him— he would paint that portrait. He would transfigure that face from the hard-glazed, cold, colourless offspring of a machine into the soft rose and glow of life; he would give a heart .to those eyes, and encircle their steely gleam with a . . .
kindly iris of genileet blne ; he would give' niovenlent to to the breast and the ns.l flush of pulsation to the chill hands.

Paul was now able to sit up and hop about by the aid ok a friendly crutch. Forthwith' he drew out his easel and colours; chose a canvas of a somewhat ambitious size. " I cannot potter in this case," said he ; "I must have elbow play." He knew this would be the keenest test to his powers yet, and had an instinctive feeling that an im- portant success or failure—perhaps the happiness of his life—was mysteriously involved in this effort. Ile knew be could draw, but hitherto his brush had never fully answered to his sense and feeling in colour. Very soon from the plastic lead grew the outline true and firm. Bard ' be worked by daylight, made detailed studies by gaslight, and before long had his picture in full, close grip. At this point he began to realize that while the photograph and his memory load served him wonderfully, he was becoming con- scious 0 some timidity and loss of force and spirit in his work. He needed more knowledge, and that inspiration which could only come by a fresh and closer view of the face in the life. But how could this be? He was not greatly troubled. The portrait was his passion, and he felt as a desperate man, and &etermined not to be baulked. I think I have not yet told the reader that Mr. Lucas, the father, had early called upon Paul to formally thank him for hie timely aid to his daughter. At this juncture (immensely lucky, Paul said) he called a second time to say that they had heard from the doctor he was no ,v able to get about, that Mrs. LICAS ennt her warm compliment?, and would he favour her with his company to dinner. The offer was readily accepted. Paul went and returned. He discovered that Mr. Lucas hell a lucrative office in the Customs that apparently he was, if not affluent, at least well-to-L ; that the house was tastefully appointed, the people in it well read, musical, and abreast of the current topics of literature and art. Indeed, he had spent a most charming evening. Before leaving our friend eagerly ac- cepted an invitation to come again, and went in about ten days. The reader will have long ago guessed the state of Paul's mind, or rather his heart. He himself, more especially since his visit, had come to know it also, lie had felt be. tore that visit it was a trifle absurd and risky to get so pre- cious "soft " on a photograph, a blush, and a dozen of thanks, and when working away at his canvas his solilo- quies would Oft shape themselves thus, "Was she affectionate? Was she companionable, good, brave, true, noble in spirit at teat times 2' Adjective rather grand and flue Mr. Paul, 'tie well you added yet— Not too bright and good For human nature's daily rood, Fur tran.lent sorrows, simple wiles, Praise, blame, love, kisses, tears, and smiles." That was one side. There was another—yes ano-her which, ever since his visit, at least, had tugged doggedly at his heart with certain queries. Could he ever hope to make her care for him ? Would she have him even if she did ? Him, a poor beggarly obscure felow of an artist. No! no!! A starving student only, his home a garret, his income a dwinning pittance, with nought in the wide earth or hsaven but a pair of stout lungs and an honest pulse under his vest. But the portrait—how comes it along? Let us step to the easel. Ha ! Pad never did work like this before. The drawing is fearless, true, and flowing. The bead stands for- ward with superb effect. Some might not consider the face beautiful ; many, and the most ctpable, would at once pro- nounce it beautiful, and all would agree it was a striking face. Its greatest charm was not revealed to the multitude ; it lay in a certain " Romola "-like queenliness with the least tinge of a pensive air. In truth she bad loved un- worthily—it had departed, but with a mark, and here hangs I a atory. Now, excepting in the face, and this he had unconsciously glorified, the artist had cast off all semblance to the customary dress and habit of his original ; a portrait it would be, but a pic- ture too. Ile would paint what he saw, but oh ! thrice over must he paint what he felt, and so it grew a poem and a song, a sweet and dreamy phantasy of colour. He had enrobed the form in huesand tints of softest harmonies, with here and there a brilliant dash of glowing colour. Now in respect to his secret, Paul was timid and blushful as a woman, and unless aided by some happy accident be was not sure he could ever speak it out. A bright thought one morning flashed to his relief. His picture should speak for him and whisper his secret and his love, and so he bung around her form with deft grace two garlands bright and. ; one he plucked wild from the hedges and meadows fresh in beauty untamed ; the other of richer hue from tended vase and garden parterre. These he linked and ringed in dalliance and embrace and mysterious tale of floral tongue (wherein they both were learned), of tender plead- ing, hope, chivalrous devotion, all-conquering love, of jo- biliant victory and wild joy. 'What," you ask, "is he going to do with his grand pic- ture? Never fear—he has had a long whip in band. All along he has meant it to hang in the coming exhibition of the Royal Academy. A scruple bothered him—he had no permission, and it did not suit his plans to seek it. Besides, there was no time—he bad put th,s off too long; it must go in for judgment to-morrow, or "too late" would be its doom, and that ignominy he would assuredly not have. Go it must, and go it did—it passed the terrible ordeal;was hung, and near the line took the fancy, on private view day, of a publisher, who offered a handsome suns tor its copyright. It was praised by ihe critics. Its name was--well, wait just one minute. He quite knew there was a sort of desperate recklessness about all this, but "Perhaps," said he, "none but 114 will be quite sure who it is." What are those invisible messengers, those ever watchful friends (ministrants of a kindly Providenc,, surely-) atten- dant on Us, who hear the unbreathed sigh, the silent, secret, musings of the heart, and with fleet wing convoy them, maybe. across the hemispheres, to thtt other--that only other heart; and so two brings love, the answering love un- known to each until the ripe time comes when it is ordained it shall be known to both? Come with me to the R A. It is early in May, the birds are yet busy and merry in love and song. You see the same trio who met so queerly at the Grosvenor last Valentine's Day. The old lady gets tired; she will rest. Paul and her daughter can come to her in about a quarter of an hour. (Thrice blessed Paul, how the angels do fling their golden haps and chances at his feet!) They saunter into the next I gallery, and stop before a picture. It is catalogued "My Valentine." There is a start—a blush—the story is read through and through in sixty seconds, and in sixty more the answer is revealed. Ah ! happy pair, God's greatest—His best—benison is yours. Worthy love requited, deep and true and pure— cherish it well, and go your way. His picture introduced him to a widening circle of friends and commissions, and when he felt entitle 4 to put and pressed a little question, she fixed the wedding for this—St. Valentine's Day.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- I put out to grass.—(Signed) THOMAS CROOK, Tytherton, I Dec. 3rd, 1789."—Agricultural Gazette. CULTURE, Xc. -- AGRICULTURAL PRODUCE STATISTICS. The agricultural department has issued statistics con- cerning the yield of the cereal and other principal crops in Great Britain in the year 1884. The data were ob- tained through estimators specially selected for the work. -England and Wales together produced a wheat brop of rather more than 77,867,000 bushels, at an esti-1 ' mated average rate of 29.85 bushels per acre, or 1.19 'bushels above the estimated ordinary average yield. For Scotland the estimated total produce amounts to 2,348,000 bushels, at an average rate of 341.7 bushels per acre, or I:48 bushels above the estimated ordinary average yield. The sum total of the results for wheat in Great Entain is thus brought up altogether to 83,215,000 bushels, the estimated average rate being 29.96 bushels per acre, or 11.9 bushels per here above the normal stan- dard of production. Of the quality of wheat produced in England and Wales more than two-fifths were grown in the group comprising the eastern and parts of certain north-eastern counties. As regards the difference shown in the yield of the cereals in the separate sections of the country, the fact, observed in preceding years, appears also in these tables, that the estimated ordinary average yield per acre in the Scotch area under wheat was 1 greater than in either of the divisions in England. The districts in which the barley and oat crops are chiefly produced, and the comparatively limited extent under wheat, together with the relatively large area under the oat crop in Scotland, as compared with the rest of Great Britain are also equally noticeable. It would thus ap- pear that, in accordance with anticipation, and apart from the slight gainlipon the ordinary standard for bar- ley, wheat is the only corn crop of the year which shows an increased average yield per acre. Of the other corn crops, barley, and contrary to some less sanguine views expressed during harvest, turns out slightly above a standard average, the produce being as variable as that of the wheat crop. The yield of barley in Great Britain has been 73,912,000 bushels, the ordinary average rate per acre being only exceeded by .06 of a bushel. The estimated average yield per acre of the oat crop falls short of that of ordinary years by 1.51 bushels, the rate of the present year in Great Britain being only 37.52 bushels per acre, with an aggregate pro- duce of 109,397,000 bushels, of which 36,713.000 bushels were grown in Scotland at an average yield per acre of 35.10 bushels, or -73 of a bushel per acre below the esti- mated ordinary production. The pulse crops have suf- fered in most localities, owing, it is stated, to aphides, and to the continued drought, which appears to have interfered with the produce of all crops other than that of wheat. Both peas and beans are considerably under the normal rate of yield. Among the root crops potatoes give the only satisfactory results as to the yield, and they are almost universally stated Ito be of excellent quality and nearly free from disease. The rate of yield, namely-6-62 tons per acre, has exceeded that of the Average of years by .51 of a ton, and shows a gross pro- duce over Great Britain of 3,743,000 tons, or 15 per cent. above the average production. The statements as to the influence of the unusually dry season upon the oat and pulse crops, apply with equal if not greater force to the yield of the root crops other than potatoes, that of turnips having turned out, as was fully anticipated, much below the average, while mange' presents a greater deficiency, excepting in Scotland, where the average yield per acre has been exceeded by 1.55 tons. The acreage 'under this crop is, however, there relatively un- important. The decrease in Great Britain from the ordinary standard was 1.97 tons per acre for turnips, and 2-87 tons per acre for mange's, the total produce amounting to 27,073,000 tons and 5,557,000 tons respec- tively. Turning now to the differences disclosed by a com- parison of the figures relating to these principal crops in Great Britain in 1884 with the estimated oldinerY (iv- age yield per acre, the results for 1884 show a decrease in each case, except in wheat, barley, and potatoes. The average rate Of wheat increased by 11.9 bushels per acre, that of barley by 0.06 of a bushel, and that of i tatoes by 0 decreased 151 of a ton. The rate for oats decreed P5l bushels per acre, the diminution in pep being 31 , ,and beans 4.51 bushels per acre, while turnips and man- gel decreased by 1.97 and 2.87 tons per acre respectively. The gross produce in 1884, as compared with the tett- mated ordinary yearly average of the decennial period above referred to, shows in cereal crops an estimated decrease in wheat of 7,756,000 bushels, or nearly 9 per cent., the diminution in the extent gown in 1884 from the average of the ten years having been not less than 380,700 acres. For barley there appears to be 8,889,000 bushels less, or nearly 11 per cent., the material factor being here likewise the very considerable decrease in the acreage under the grain. In oats, on the other hand, notwithstanding the diminished rate of yield in the pre- sent year, we find the total produce in 1884 has ex- ceeded that of the yearly average of the Period referred to by 1,385,000 bushels, or about 1 per cent., the area sown having been greater by 147,700 acres. For peas -the diminution in the estimated total production, as compared with the period in question, would appear to be 2,103,000 bushels, the decrease in beans being 2,939,000 bushels. In the other crops for 1884 similarly compared there is an estimated increase of 490,000 tons in potatoes, while turnips and mange' have decreased by 4,565,000 and 1,295,000 tons resnectivele

"NOTE FROM THE FTLDE.—A PROIFIC Cow.—An agri- cultural correspondent from the-Kirkham district says: On Tuesday, 27th January, a cow belonging to Mr. Ralph Milner, Dowbridge, near Kirkham, was delivered of three full-grown, well-developed heifer calves. Ou the Thurs- day afterwards, the cow dropped another substance, which on examination was found to be a fourth calf,but of a most peculiar character. It consisted of a small oval bag or pouch, about 4in. by 3in. The skin (of which this monstrosity was principally•composed) was principally covered with hair, almost precisely similar in colour and marking to the other three calves, all of which bore an almost cact resemblance to each other. The cow, which is a well-bred shorthorn, was only nine days from her full term' and has given birth to seven calves previously all in the ordinary 'course, is recover- ing. The calves were all dead. CO-OPERATIVE AGILICOLTURE.—WO are promised an- other experiment in co-operative agriculture, which may be said to begin under favourable auspices, inasmuch as Sir Thomas Brassey, who is about to institute it, is not only an excellent man of business, but also a zealous and experienced co-operator. Speaking at Hastings last week, Sir Thomas said that, like other landlords, he feels the pinch of agricultural depression in the shape of un- tenanted holdings. The proper party to call in to his assistance, under these circumstances, he holds to be "the peasant farmer." Accordingly, he means to see what petite culture, combined with co-eperation, will do for him. In making the announcement, Sir Thomas re- ferred to similar experiments made some time ago at Glynde by the present Lord Hampden. 'So far as the speaker's words serve as an indication of his plan, he intends to proceed on similar lines, although at Glynde they did not, if we recollect right, lead to absolute suc- cess. The principle to be adopted appears to be that of profit sharing rather than that of 'joint enterprise with proportionately equal risks, and co-operation, in this sense, rather between the landlord and each individual tenant than between the tenants. collectivebr,las; at As- sington.—Sussex Advertiser. THE DEMANDS OF THE SCOTTISH FARMERS' ALLIANCE. —A large number of farmers from all parts of Scotland attended the atinual meeting of the Scottish Farmers' I Alliance held at Aberdeen last week, a deputation from the English Alliance also being prdkent. The meeting was a great Success, and its result was the adoption, with very little alteration, of the proposals made by the committee of the association. The objects, as amended by the committee, and further amended in one particular at the annual meeting, are briely and clearly expressed. The most important addition Is the object demanding the institution of a Land Court in every county in Scot- land to arbitrate in matters of dispute between landlord and tenant. Another object, as proposed by the com- mittee, asked for the abolition of the Game Laws as far as arable land is concerned, and the restriction of the area of deer forests and grouse moors; but the limita- tion as to arable land was voted out by a large majority at the meeting, and the Scottish Alliance now stands committed to the total abolition of the Game Laws. Other objects of great importance were those in favour of rating plantations, shooting, and fishing at their full annual value, whether let or urdet, and of a representa- tive system of local government. At the present time in Scotland shootings, if held by the owners, are not rated at all, and when they are let they are only rated at their supposed net value, after deducting all the ex- penses of keeping them up. This is a gross injustice, as I there is no reason why sporting rights should net be assessed on the same basis as farms, whether the owner enjoys them or lets them. the first resolution declared the need of freedom of cultivation and sale of produce, security for improvements and " cestainty " of tenure, to enable farmers to meet foreign competition. The second resolution declared the need of a new Act, which will provide, among other things, for the establishment of Land Courts to arbitrate Intween landlord and tenant as to the couditiOns under which land is to be held, and to provide small holdings for labourers where desirable. The third resolution ',demands a measure to be passed next Session to break current leases, which threaten the ruin of a large proportion of the farmers of Scotland. IThe repeal of all Acts bearing on the land," th 'make way for the proposed new Land Act, was also asked for, the intention bemg chiefly to get rid of the Agricultural Holdings Act. RIPENING CREA.I4.;—Mr. John Gould, Ontario, Canada, writes in an American contemporary as follows :—" Heat is not very often employed in cream ripening, its oppo- site, low temperature being considered the best plan. If heat is employed, it is usually used to scald the milk. This should never be done. To scald milk is to make the cheesy matter in the milk to some extent lighter than the butter fats, and a leathery, wrinkly scum ap- pears, which contains but a small percentage of cream. It at last finds its way into the butter, increasing its weight with cheese fats—not butter fats—and causing an increased solidity. Cream is not improved by being held at a low temperature for several days to sour? One of the most prolific causes of cream not coming is in having it kept at 40 deg. to 50 deg., and then warmed up to 60 deg., and churned. If this cream had been warmed up, and kept at about 80 deg. until a slight acidity began to assert itself, and then cooled down to 58 deg. and churned, we get the effect of ripening has- tened by bringing the oxygen of the air to our aid, rather than the carbonic acid souring at a low tempera- ture. There is a great difference between the ripened stage of acidity from the oxygen of the air and that of souring as a result of lactid acid development. Oxygen- of the air, when brought into contact with cream at about 80 deg., converts some of the volatile oils of butter into flavour. We thus escape the dangers of changing the sugar of the milk into an element that makes the lactic acid conspicuous, and we get the sharp flavour characteristic of sour cream butter, but which after all is not true butter flavour. With heat to rapidly pro- mote this ripening quality, cream is made more uniform in quality than by any other process. The oxygen reaches every part of the cream readily, and by its powerful and rapid action promotes uniformity of con- dition. SHIRE HORSES.—In the first of a series of Horse papers, an Australian agricultural jo,urnal says :—The advent amongst us of .notable specunens of the "shire" horse is likely to arouse some of the spirit of contention and discussion which have been animating admirers of draught stock in the old land. The horses of the shire type seen here, so far, leave scarcely .a doubt of their origin. They are an outcome of careful breeding, in which mares of repute from England—English cart mares, in fact—were put to Clydesdale stallions. The results, if the reports of late years are to be credited, are somewhat startling—not a few of the " shire " men claiminc,o that they show horses that are improvements upon the original sires. Indeed, it was stated at a recent meeting of notables in London, called for the purpose of establishing a society to amalgamate the stud books of the Clvdesdale9 and English cart horse, that an English horse—Lincolnshire Lad—was the sire of many of the best prize-winning Clydesdales in Scotland. The statement has aroused much amusement; but it is not correct, although it is true that Lincolnshire Lad is credited with the parentage of not a few of the prize- winners in the Scotch agricultural horse classes of the last half-score years, but these animals do not, in the stud-book sense, rank as Clydesdales. Having seen so many really line animals claiming Lincolnshire Lad as either sire or grandsire exhibited in Scotland, some people north of the Tweed have naturally become anxious to see such a marvellously good getter and grand wearer as that horse must be. If they knew exactly where the fine old horse was to be seen, they would go a little out of their way to inspect him. His stock, how- ever, good as many of them are, do not possess the qualifications for entry in the Clydesdale Stud-book. It is, therefore, a mistake to speak of them as Clydesdales in the same breath almost as reference is made to stud- books. Mr. Pole-Gel has recently alluded to the drain of England's best mares and Allies away to Scotland for breeding purposes. It has no doubt been eonSiderable, and has imparted size and substance to many Scotch- bred horses; but we imagine ills not now so great as it. FAIL'S RENTS IN THE PENRITII DISTRICT.-It is stated that farmers in the Penrith district have for some time past been seriously considering the question of a reduc- tion of farm rents; and in the belief that landlords ought, in some measure, to share the burdens of the tenants, they have determined to call, on an early date, a mass meeting of farmers for the purpose of consider- ing and discussing the whole subject of agricultural de- pression and rent reduction. REARING CALvus.—Circumstances have led us to ex- amine for a special purpose all the books connected with agriculture which we can find dated prior to 1828.. It has been a cause of no small surprise to discover how many so-called modern inventions are really old prac- tices revived. From the "Universal Magazine," pub- lished July, 1790, we take the following. It is stated to be "a letter written to the secretary of the Bath Agri- culture," by which, we suppose, reference is intended to the veteran society now commonly described as the Bath and West of England Society:—" The following is my calculation of the expense of rearing calves without milk :—ln the year 1787 I weaned 17; in 1788 I weaned 23, and 15 in 1789. I bought in 1787 three sacks of lin- seed; I put one quart of seed to six qparts of water, and boil it 10 minutes, when it becomes h jelly. This jelly is mixed with a small quantity of tea of the best hay steeped in boiling water. Having my calves drop at different times, I did not make my calculation of the cost of hay-tea; but out of my three sacks of seed, I have now left better than two bushels. I gave the calves jelly and hay-tea three times a day, and 6d. a day to the boy who looked after them. The price of the linseed was 4s. 6d. per bushel, or £2 ss. for the three seasons. My calves are kept in a good •growing state, and are better at this minute than my neighbours', which were reared with milk, not having fallen away so much when

TITE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. POULTRY HOUSES FOR FARMERS.

A question is very often asked as to which is the best kind of housojor poultry, for there are many kinds which have at various times been recommended. There can be no question that where the rich amateur wishes to have a poultry yard which, in respect to its build- ings and appearance, will do credit to himself and to his purse that the best one, is a large house, divided into a number of separate dwellings, with a passage up the centre and a row of roosting places on either side. We have seen such places as these, and they may be called the "drawing-rooms" of poultry keeping. But these bear the same relationship to what is necessary as do the elaborate byres of the cow fancier or the.swell stables of the horse keeper to the more modest but not less com- fortable dwellings on the farm. Such places may do for those who are willing to pay well for their hobbies, and I we do not deny but that they may obtain much addi- tional pleasure out of the pursuit because of the style hi which it is carried out. But when profit is the object, every sovereign spent unnecessarily is a handicap on success. We wish, therefore, to now consider what is the best kind of poultry house for the farmer. If the circumstances of every farm were alike, it would not be difficult to decide what was the best to suggest, but as this is not the case, varying conditions have to be met. Thus, in districts where hunting is common and foxes abound, precautions have to be taken against these enemies of the poultry keeper. And 1 in thickly-populated districts, especially where manu- factories or mines draw together large masses of men, some of whom are not marked by any sense of right and wrong, it is needful to guard against what they may do. Happy is the poultry keeper who is neither troubled oy biped or quadruped, and he is enabled to do that which his less fortunate friend may not. To any farmer who can put his fowls out without fear, the most suitable house is a small one holding from a dozen to a score birds. This house should be about five feet square, and about four feet high inside. But, if pos- sible, the floor should stand about 30 inches above the ' ground, so as to form a shelter beneath.for the birds. Such a house can be made by a handy man at home for 355. or 405., and is none the worse if made of unplaned deals. It can either be put on wheels which will add somewhat to the expense, or be made with wooden , handles, so that it can be moved by a couple of men.

THE PYNAMIII PLOT. , CUNNINGHAM AND BURTON AT BOW-STREET. At Bow-street Police Court, before Sir James Ingham, on Monday, the two prisoners James Gilbert Cunningham, 22, described as a dock labourer, and Harry Burton, described as a carpenter or cabinet maker, were charged on remand with having been concerned with maliciously causing an explosion at the Tower of London on the 24th ult. The court was strongly guarded by police, it being stated that there were not less than 500 officers and men in and about the premises.—Mr. Poland, as before, prosecated on behalf of the Crown, there being else, present Mr. A.-K. Stephen- son, solicitor to the Treasury ; the Hon. H. Cuffe, and Mr. Pollard, from the same department. • - Mr. Poland, for the prosecution, stated that it would be shown that Cunningham arrived in Liverpool from New York on December 20th. Oa December 24t1e he was in Landon, and thus his statement of leaving worked for two months at the Liverpool Docks was shown to be false. He brought a brown American trunk with him, which he re- moved to London, but which disappeared for a time. It would be shown that the trunk was secretly taken from Great Prescott-street to 90, Turner's-road, Bow, where the other prisoner, Barpn, lodged. Burton arrived at Liver- pool on Christmas Eve, and came to Loudon next day. Beth men took lodgings in the neighbourhood of the rower, Burton in Mitre-square, close to Aldgate Station, and Cun- ningham in Great Prescott-street. Burton had been under the observation of the pr lice for some days. and was seen in the company of Cunningham on January 18th. There was no question that this treasonable conspiracy had its head- quarters in America. Men come over to this country from time to time with Atlas dynamite, and attacked public buildiregs in London. It was a somewhat curious fact that the "dock labourer" Cunningham and the " carpenter " or " cabinetmaker." Burton were both in London in the spring of last year. Cunningham came over in May and remained here for some time. He started from New York I think on May 9th, and he was pro- bably in this country when at soy We one of the ex- plosions took place at Scotland-yard and at the Junior Carlton Club, and when the dynamite was found at the Nelson Column. That was on May 30th. He then went back to America. How he could afford to make these jour- neys, being only a dock labourer, the magistrate would be able to form an opinion. But it was also a curious coinci- dence that the other man, Burton, was also in this country in the spring of last year, and be was here about March. He was certainly here, continuing on for some time, for he went to St. Bartholomew's Hospital, and was attended there in July. He returned to America in September, and here was this cabinetmaker back in this country in December. It was another curious coincidence that each man came to live near to the other, and in the neighbourhood of the Tower, and it was also a curious coincidence that very soon after these two men had arrived, namely, on January 2nd of this year, an explosion of dynamite took place at a little after nine o'clock at night on the Metropolitan Railways in the tunnel between King's Cross and Gower-street Stations. It was also a curious coincidence that the train started from Aldgate, within a few hundred yards of the place were Harry Burton lived, and aleo within a few minutes' walk of the place were Cunningham and his friend W4EO also liv- ing. When That explosion took place and the lights were blown out and the train came to a standstill at Gower-street Station, a constable ran down from the street. Connected with the train was a spare brake, in which passengers some- times ride, and in that spare brake, which was one carriage away from the engine, there were some men, one of whom was undoubtedly the prisoner Cunningham and another was Harry Burton. The constable who came down the steps lost sight of them, and they managed to make their escape in the confusion that ensued upon the explosion, and the subsequent screaming of women and children. The evi- dence was accumulating .from day to day, but at present there was undoubtedly the fact that Cunningham was in the Tower at the time of the - explosion. When Burton was taken into custody and his luggage searched, there was found upon him a guide to the Tower, and he admitted that he had since his last visit to this country, when he went to Mitre-square, visited the Tower. It was also a coincidence that there was found upon him a guide-book relating to the new Palace at Westminater. The learned counsel, in conclu- sion, commented on the numerous falsehoods told by the prisoners in their statements to the police. Evidence bearing out the opening statement was given. and Dr. Dupre said the detonator found in Cunningham's box could not be purchased retail, and would not cause an explosion without dynamite. It transpired that a police. constable lodged at the same house as Burton, and, being suspicious of the latter, he made a report, as a result of which a plain clothes officer was told off to watch Burton. This officer saw the two prisoners meet one day in the street, walk together, and stand engaged in conversation for several minutes. He afterwards picked Cunningham out in the police cells, and Burton from among hill-a-dozen other misonere. The statement of Burton with regard to the trunk previously believed tre have been in Cunningham's possession was read. He said he met a man in the street carrying the trunk. He (Burton) askeel him if he wanted to sell it. The man said he did, and he bought the trunk for Bs. He did not think it strange to buy a box in that way. Burton's late landlady said be told her he was going to bring a trunk, and she agreed that it would be best to go in the corner of the bedroom which he pointed out. When he brougfit the trunk he did not say where he had obtained it. The prisoners were both remaadeel for another week, Burton asking to be allowed a copy of a daily paper.
