THE SOUDAN CA.IVIPAIGN.
DEATH OF GENERAL GORDON.

TERRIBLE MASSACRES IN KHARTOUM. GAE.DI3I4, FEB. 8.—Unfortunately no doubt can now exist that General Gorden was among those mas- sacred when Khartoum fell into the hands of the rebels. Natives who escapeo describe him as having been killed in coming out of his house to rally his faithful troops, who were taken by surprise. They were out down to a man. • For hours the best part of the town was the scene of a merciless massacre. Even the women and children were not spared. All the notables, except thaireaoherous Pitches and their followers, were put to the sword. All this seemed too probable from the first, when Sir Charles Wilson with his steamers went up as far Tutti, and saw beyond the trees that the island and the streets of Khartoum and plains outside were anywheredi n gthe Had a crowded with dervishes with flaunting banners, and no friendly sign was given from the palace or Egyp- tianfortified monastery, as some averred, ha would certainly have fired some ednaGordonignw aßblieenyinhgol shots as a signal to.tho steamers. Gordon's other boats and nuggara were seen.lying beside the banks on the Omdurman side, which was occupied by rebels. In coming down both steamers got safely through the Great Gate Cataract, but were wrecked on the island just below. Kashim Elmoos Gordon's most trusted officer, was true to the last, hilt doubts wore entertained of the i fidelity of Abdul Ahmed, the Second n command, and he justified these by deserting.—Daily Nam (REUTERS TELEGRAM 'Conn, FEB. 8, IT 30 rzr —Sir Charles Wilson and Lieutenant Stuart Wortley have arrived here from Gubat, having made the journey in four days. They bring intelligence of General Gordon's death on Feb• ruary 61. th. A messenger from Colonel Boscawen at Gnbat has arrived here bringing details of the fall of Khartoum. He states that one of the treacherous Paellas marched the Khartoum Garrison to the Omdurman side of the city, telling them that an attack of the Mandi's troops I was expected there. Meanwhile the other Pachas opened the gates of Khartoum, allowing the rebels to enter. The messenger adds that General Gordon was stabbed while leaving the Government House. The Press Association says that the statements which were published on Wednesday morning from various corres- pondents in Egypt that General Gordon had been killed on the night of the capture of Khartoum by the Mabdi created a profound sensatioe. For the greater part of the day the news was generally held to be conclusive that he had fallen a victim to the treachery of the Egyptian soldiers. Many Inquiries were directed during the afternoon to the War Office and other sources of information seeking further confirmation or details, but none were forthcoming. In fact in consequence of the circula•ion of a statement by some of the evening newspapers that a despatch had been received by Lord Wolseley stating that a scout despatched to Khar- I town by Colonel Boscawen had returned with intelligence I confirming Gordon's death, the War Office issued a dis- claimer announcing that no such telegram had been received at the War Offices up to 3 p.m. When definite news is re- ceived at the War Office concerning General Gordon's fate it will be immediately communicated to the Dress. The official announcement has to some extent reassured the pub- lie mind, but the gravest fears are still entertained for the gallant General's safety.

THE FATE OF GORDON: HIS DEATH CONFIRMED. The following despatch has been received from Lord Wolseley : KORTI, THURSDAY MoiniNG.—Up to date have no re- liable particulars about Gordon's fate. The press reports are based on rumours gathered by Wilson's party when de- scending the Nile from Omdurman to Gubat, The Mudir and all the natives persist that Khartoum has not fallen, but Wilson is positive, and there can be little doubt on the point. Hope in a few days to have back the messengers Sent to ascertain the facts. (From General Lord Wolseley to Secretary of State.) KORTI, THURSDAYt 10-15 p.m.—No 75. Following re- ceived from Generalßrackenbury: KEIMEXAN, WEDNESDAY.—The following is a translation of a document found to-day by a private soldier of the Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry in a donkey's saddle bag about 400 yards behind the position we captured yesterday. The document begins A copy of a letter received from the Governor-General of Berber to the Governor of the section. In the name of God, &c. From Mahommed Kheir Abdullah Khoy FA Emir General of Berber, to his friend, Abdul Magid Abi el Lekalelc, and all his men. I inform you that to-day after the midday prayer we received a letter from the faithful Khalifa Abdullah Ebeu Mohammed, in which he tells Us that Khartoum was taken on Monday, the 9th Rabi, 1302, on the side of El Ilaoui in the following manner :—The Malidi prayed upon his dervishes and his troops to advance against the fortifications and entered Khartoum in a quarter of an hour. They killed the traitor Gordon and captured the steamers and boats. God has made him glorious. Be grateful and thank sod praise God for his tinspeanable mercy. I announce it to you. Tell your troops." On it is written' "received FridaY, 20th Rabi," The 9th Rabi is the 26th January.
RESCUE OF SIR C. WILSON. NARROW ESCAPE OF LORD CHARLES BERESFORD.

The following telegram from Lord Wolseley has been received by the Secretary of State for War : " Koarr, Feb. 9, 7-30 r.m.—Sir Charles Wilson Las just reached my camp, having left Gubat early on morning. of 6th-instant. General Stewart's wound well. we. Sir Charles Wilson's party all safe. Lord Obarles Bereeford, in a steamer brought him back, having engaged enemy's battery within three miles of island on which Wilson's party were landed. In action with battery, enemy's found shot went through steamer's boiler ; Beresford had to anchor under fire until he repaired boiler. "Wilson, with his four guns, ammunition, and party, landed from island on right bank, and marched down stream opposite battery, and came into action, helping with Beresford's fire on battery in keeping enemy's fire down.
"Towards sunset Wilson marched down river
MAP OF THE SEAT OF WAR.

about three miles, and halted for night. Beresford joined them in the morning, having again engaged enemy's battery in passing it, and brought them safely to Gubat. Edwin Ournow, second-class petty officer, killed; Lieutenant E. Van ICough• net, Royal Navy, wounded (iltah wound in thigh) ; and two English and four natives woun- ded or scalded in engine-room when shot went through boiler. . _ _ _

"I cannot speak too highly of plucky manner in which Lord C. Beresford acted on this occasion. Indeed, all his pay, and that under Sir C. Wil- son, behaved admirably, and with the usual deter- mination of Englishmen." [From the Daily News] GAKIRTL, FEBRUARY B.—Sir Charles Wilson, Captain Trafford, and twenty of the Sussex Regiment, with 320 of Gordon's faithful Soudanese, remained on the Wand for three days, and were rescued by Lord Charles Beresford's steamer on Tuesday last. In going up Lord Charles briskly encountered the enemy's troops manning the earth works and semi-circular redoubt at the foot of the cataract. Early in the morning a shot from the battery struck the boiler, and the steamer lay-to disabled under a heavy fire until nightfall. Lord Charles Bereaford's gunners, however, threw shells into the embra- sure, disabling one of the enemy's guns, and so swept these with the fire of the gatlings that they completely silenced the battery. Our Melted marksmen at 800 yards range poured such accurate fire Into the trenches that the enemy could not reply. . _

Sir Charles. Wilson with Major Stuart Wortley and an escort of the Camel Regiment, arrived at Gado! from On- bat last night, and left for Korti in the morning. AN EMISSARY OF THE MARDI IN ENGLAND.—A STRANGE STORY. _

A clergyman Itoldini-a--cii;tinitaiijeci—position in London gives a very extraordinary statement respecting the nature and movements of the Mandi's emissaries in England : " About three months ago I first made the acquaintance, at an hotel near Victoria Station, of an Egyptian gentleman, an ex-Pacha. One day, about the beginning of December, I approached him with the object of ascertaining his nation- ality. We spoke in French on general topics, and almost daily afterwards I met him on the beet of terms. I dis- covered that my companion was none other than the Pref6t de Police at Cairo during the temporary reign of Arabi, and had actually helped to conceal Arabi after the battle of ' Tel-el-Kebir. The Mandi, he said, had arranged to allow Wolseley to approach Khartoum. He might offer fight near Shendy with a portion of his troops, in order to tempt Wolseley to greater risk, but would ou no account fight a decisive battle until the forces were concentrated in or around Khartoum. General Gordon, he affirmed, was al- ready virtually a prisoner in the Mandes hands, the 'de- fence of Khartoum ' being a mere form, and no sooner were the English troops within a days' march of the citadel than he would enter into possession, and fight Wolseley from the point of vantage. This was stated to ma more than once in confidence between Christmas and the end of the first week of January. Other details he gave me of lesser impor- tance, but he said times without number that Gordon would not be killed. Instead of Lord Wolseley relieving Khar- toum and Gordon, the Mandi, he said, would do so; and the Mandi will make you pay through the nose for Gordon.'"

On Friday night Professor Malden, F.G.S., addressing the Wolverhampton Scientific Society, on the Soudan, ex- pressed his strong conviction that certain of the recent let- ters purporting to have been despatched by Gordon, were forgeries by the Mandi. Three weeks ago he inspccted at Chichester letters in the possession of Miss Gordon sup- posed to have come from Khartoum. They were on very thin paper, no larger than a visiting c.trd, and had been sewn up in the desert messenger's wristband. He than be- lieved they were forgeries, and the fall of Khartoum strengthened his suspicions. GENERAL EARLE'S ADVANCE ON BERBER.—A SKIRMISH.-30 ARABS KILLED.

BIRTI, SATURDAY (VIA. MERAWI, SUNDAY.)—The enemy has at length been found. The Camel Corps, while skir- mishing a few miles inland, on Thursday last, came upon a body of the rebels around the Wells. Our men speedily opened fire, which the rebels returned, but the fight they made was comparatively poor, and the wells were soon in our possession. Thirty of the enemy were found to have been shot and lay upon the field. Six of the rebels were captured unwounded. Besides this, a large number of Remington rifles, camels, and cattle fell into our hands. Two of the prisoners who were examined declared that a distinguished officer of Osman Digma, who had been pro- moted for special bravery in the neighbourhood of Suakim, was in command of the force. Our casualties are trifling. The rebels were effectually dispersed by the charge of our troops. The Camel Corps is now returning to Shakoob with their booty. (From the Daily Yews) BIRTER, FEB. 7TD.—The Duke of Cornwall's regiment has arrived here. The Gordon Highlanders passed the Mishani Cataract, and bad to portage the boats and stones. The river is becoming lower and worse every day. They could not ascend the same passiges we did. The camels scouting to the front came on some natives guarding cattle. They exchanged shots and drove off the enemy, killing about four. They took six camels and 16 head of cattle and some boats. The 13th Gordon Highlanders have arrived at Mora. Grain is still being found about Bide!). Salle- man's property here has been destroyed. His uncle Abuliekes and Tarki, prominent Shagiyeh rebels, have come in, and are now prisoners here. The health of the troops is good. There are thirteen sick. BIRTED, FEB. Orer.—The advance was resumed yesterday. The Staffords went up the river in the afternoon. The Hussars found the enemy in a good position, and exchanged shots with them. The cavalry returned to camp in the evening LARGE REINFORCEMENTS ORDERED.—THE GUARDS AND INDIAN TROOPS TO BE SENT OCT. An unusually protracted meeting of the Cabinet was held on Saturday, at the Prints Minister's official residence, Downing-street. The deliberations of the Ministers began at twelve noon, and did not conclude until twenty minutes to four. It is understood that Ira reply to a long telegram sent to Lord Wolseley on the previous afternoon by the Secretary of State for War, further messages in cypher and Of a confidential character received at an early hour by wire from his Lordship were submitted. As soon as the Cabinet had concluded, additional Instructions were telegraphed to the General Commanding in the Soudan, and such informa- tion given to the responsible heads of the military depart- ments in this country as to guide them in the arrangements necessary for promptly and effectively carrying out the. course which Lord Wolseley regards as most likely, both to achieve the rescue of Gorden, if still alive, which is the primary object in view, and at the same time to inflict die. comfiture upon the Matadi. The general belief is that actiye operations at Suakim, and the opening of the desert route from that port to Berber, are among the contemplated operations. A Council of War was held on Saturday evening at the

Admiralty. Lord Hartington arrived at the official resi- dence of the First Lord of the Admiralty shortly after five p m,from the War Office. His Lordship and Lord Northbro6k were shortly afterwards joined by Mr. Childers The deliberations of the Ministers lasted nearly two hours. It is understood that the object of consideration was the despatch of reinforcements required. by Lord Wolseley, especially by theSualcim and Berber route. The Admiralty authorities are now in a position without delay to transport to' the Red Sea, if required, an Army Corps. Another long sitting of Cabinet Ministers took place on Monday afternoon. There is reason to believe that the pro- posals of the Government with regard to the financial affairs of Egypt chiefly occupied attention. At three o'clock on Monday, an hour after the assembling of the Cabinet, the Government, with the sanction of her Majesty, gave their authority to Lord Wolseley's demand for the despatch of a large number of troops to reinforce him. This decision was at once forwarded by special rnes- senger to the acting Adjutant-General at the War Office (General Sir Arthur Herbert), who, having anticipated such orders, had previously instructed cettain regiments which formed part of the First Army Corps, and are therefore up to full war strength, to hold themselves in readiness for almost immediate embarkation for service in the Soudan. The route to the Nile by way of Suakim and Berber appears to have been definitely adopted, as in most cases where troops have been ordered on foreign service Suakim has been named as their destination. The most important order Promulgated was that directing that three battalions of Foot Guards should prepare for foreign service. These are the Ist Battalion Coldstream Guards, quartered at Welling- ton Barracks •, 2nd Battalion Scots Guards, quartered at Wellington and Kensington Barracks; and the 3rd Battalion Grenadier Guards, quartered at Windsor. They have been directed to be ready within a few hours' notice, and the men were medically examined and weaker men rejected. The 3d Grenadiers and Ist Coldstreams returned from the Crimea in June, 1856, and the 2od Scots from Canada in 1864. The Guards have to tie in readiness to start from Albert Docks to day (Satiteday). They will be conveyed direct to Suakim, when they will take part in the epedj. dit ion to open the road to Berber. Orders were also received at Aldershot that the remaining section of the Royal Engineers, 3rd Battalion Rifle Brigade, numbering 24 officers and 800 men; 20th Hussars, to the number of eight officers. 250 men, and 300 horses ; 13th Company of Commissariat and Transport Corps, under Captain Stokes, number 130 men, and a detachment ef the Medical Staff, should prepare for foreign aervice immedi- ately. The let Battalion Devonshire Regiment, 800 strong, stationed at Newry, received c rders on Monday morning to be in readiness to proceed to Egypt. The men were at once paraded and inspected. Orders were received by the Medical Staff in Woolwich to prepare medical stores for ten thousand men. Pharmacy waggons marked field hos- pitals, 2nd army corps, are now on the Arsenal Wharf. On Monday, at a late how: order?) were received at Daven- port that the 3rd Company of the Transport and Commis- ' sariat Corps was to prepare for ils deparitite to Egypt. In addition to the foregoing, the let Battalian Highland Light Infantry and the 2nd Battalion Royal Dublin Fusiliers will proceed to Egypt from Gibraltar, and the Zed Battalion Royal Sussex Regiment and the let Battalion Yorkshire Regiment will be despatched from Cairo to Suakim. It is stated that the force to form this new expedition is to number 7,000 of all ranks, made up as follows :—Firat Battalion of Coldstreams, Second Battalion Scots Guards, and Third Battalion Grenadier Guards, 750 each; Cavalry, about 600; Second Battalion Royal Dublin Fusiliers, 750; First Battalion Yorkehire Regiment, 600; a regiment from Malta, 700, and Other regimentsbret to be named, with Artil- lery, Engineers, commissariat, and transport corps, in addition to Marines, Blue Jackets, and other detachments already at Suakim. CAIRO, MONDAY.— The Yorkshire Regiment at Alexan- dria, and the East Surrey Regiment, at Cairo, have received orders to bold themselves in readiness to proceed at once to Suakim. Their place will be taken by the 2nd Battalion of the Durham Regiment and the let Battalion of the Stafford- shire Regiment. The G (B) Battery of the Royal Horse Artillery, and the 6 (1) Battery' of the Royal Artillery will also proceed from Cairo to Suakim. The Irish Fusiliers from Gibraltar, two regiment from Malta, and a brigade of Guards and four squsdrons of cavalry from home will make up the Suakim expeditionary force. . . .
Marines hive liem sent from Suez to Suakirn to prepare for the arrival of further troops, and the Humber, I.vhich has arrived at Suez, will be utilised in the transport of troops. . . .

It is reported that Major-Lieneral R Gipps,at present corn- mending the Home District, will be entrusted with the chief command of the Suakim-Berber expedition. The third battalion of Grenadier Guards, under Colonel Thynne, now on garrison at Windsor Castle are under orders for E;ypt. On Tuesday morning the 7th and 12th companies of the Transport Branch Cornenisariat and Trans- port Corps at Aldershot were medically inspected for the Soudan. All the Corps and departments at Aldershot are ready to leave camp at an hour's notice. THE RESERVES TO BE CALLED OUT.

The war preparations were on Wednesday cantinued with unabated vigour at Woolwich, Aldershot, and other mili- tary depots, and the equipment of the expc.ditionary corps of ten thousand men is being rapidly pushed forward. It is now decleively announced that Sir Gerald Graham, V.C., will take command of the force operating on the Suakim- Berber road, with Major-General Fremantle in command of the Guards Brigade, and Major-General Greaves as Chief of the Staff. The statement that bdian native troops would be employed in the Soudan is fully confirmed. The Mar- quis of Lansdowne has been offered the services of a regi- ment of French-Canadian volunteers, to be raised in the Dominion for employment in Flgypt or elsewhere. Arms and stores are being transmitted to a large number of depbts in the United Kingdom, to which men of the reserve will be shortly called for garrison duly. Several volunteer corps have also been placed at the disposal of the authorities for a similar purpose, if necessary. The War Office notifies . .
',hat it is prepared to accept the temporry services of a
. . . limited number of militia officers or officers in the reserve in various departments of the army. It is not improbable
that a nutnber of volunteers who have been trained in hoe-
pital and ambulance work will be asked to assist the Medi- cal Staff Corps in the field. The Guards and the 20th Hussars will it is stated, embark from the London Docks on

Wednesday next. In pursuance of the War Office instructions sent to the Tower and Pimlico to get ready arms, clothing, and accou- trements for seventy military centres prior to the issue of a Royal proclamation calling out 10,000 infantry of the reserve forces of the British army, these military necessaries are being prepared for forwarding to the infantry barracks of the under.nentioned towns, at which the reserves will be ordered to assemble for garrison and other duty during the absence of the troops required for the Soudan expeditim : —Berwick-upon-Tweed, Sunlerland, Carlisle, Richmond, Beverley, York, Pontefract, Halifax, Lancaster, Preston, Warrington, Burnley, Ashtm-und,r-Lyne, Bury, Chester,,A Lichfiekl, Shrewsbury, Worcester, Wrexhatn, Cardiff, Brecon, Derby, Leicester, Warwick, Northampton, Great Yarmouth, Bury St. Edmund;, Bedford. Exeter, Bodmin, Taunton, Bristol, Deyivs, Dorchester, Tort Elson, Wincheiter, Read- ing, Oxford, Chitier, Worley, Canterbury, Maidstone, Kingston, Guildford, Hounsiow, Inverness, Aberdeen, Perth, Stirling, Hamilton, Ayr, Glencorse, Belfast, Omagh, Naas, Birr, Galway, Clonmel, and Trate°. THE SULTAN AND THE MAHDL

- - BERLIN, WEDNESDAY.—Intelligence received here from Constantinople states that a Cabinet Council was summoned by the Sultan last Sunday evening in order to discuss the affairs of Egypt and the Soudan. The Ministers remained in Council up to a late hour without being able to arrive at a decision, in consequence of not having fall cognisance of the real state of affairs. The fall of Khartoum has canted great excitement among the Mussulmans, a large number of whom are in favour of the Mandi. The Porte regards the MalidPe victory as unfortunate for Turkey, and foresees that it may lead to complications. The semi-official Terjumahi Hakitat says the British disasters in the Soudan are the result of England's proceedings in disorganising the military element in Cairo and creating anarchy in the Egyptian administration. The journal declares that Turkey alone is able to save the British army in the Sou- dan. CONSTANTINOPLE, WEDNESDA.Y.—SffiCI orders have been given to the Turkish press to abstain from publishing any comment in regard to the state of affairs in Egypt or the Soudan. ITALIAN OCCUPATION OF MASSOWAU. ROME TUESDAY.-1 telegram from Suakim, containing details of the occupation of Massowah. states that on the arrival of the expedition Admiral Caimi went on shore to confer with the Egyptian Governor. The latter declared that he could not permit the landing of Italian troops with- out protesting. The Italian troops subsequently landed, and Occupied unopposed the town and forts. The Italian tlig was hoisted by the side of the Egyptian colours. The Italians are well received by the population. The Egyptian garrison remains in its former quarters. MOVEME.NTS AT SUAKIN'. " • ANOTHER GREAT BATTLE. GENERA. EARLE BILLED. ENEMY RGUTED WITH HEAVY LOSS. DESPATCH FROM LORD WOLSELEY. Durma ISLAND, TITESDAY.—GeneraI Earle advanced at ten o'clock this morning, with the South Staffotdshire Re- giment, the Black Watch, the Cavalry, the Camel Corps, and two guns, against a high rocky ridge to the right of the enemy's position, which rested on the river. The troops turned to the left and attacked from the mainland the rear of the enemy, who were keeping up an accurate rifle fire. The main position of the rebels on some rocky hills near the river was attacked by the Black Watch; and their Position on the centre by the Staffordshire Regiment. The troops advanced under heavy fire by rushes from one ridge to another, the enemy still holding the main position. General. Earle ordered thd Black Watch to storm the hill which was captured and carried at the point of the bayonet. General Earle then fell while leading the attack on the enemy's centre. Meanwhile two companies of the Staffordshire Regiment attacked the high ridge, and on be- ing reinforced by the remainder of the regiment carried the last position of the enemy. It was difficult to estimate the strength of the rebels, whose firing was very accurate. The enemy were composed of the l'alonaesir and Robatah tribes- men, among wham were several dervishes from Berber, Their loss was heavy, and included several emirs. The following despatch is published by the War OfAze From General Lord Wolseley to the See-...'aary of State for War. Received 12th FOres'y, dated Korti, 11th February, 1835, 11-60 Pm. The following telegram just received from General Brackenbury CAMP OPPOSITE BULK& ISLAND, TEESDAY.—Having found enemy in position stated in telegram No. 98 of 9th instant, General Earle concentra'ed Staffordshire 414 Plack Watch here yesterday, reconnoitred the position, and this morning advanced to attack it. They held a high ridge of razor-backed 12105 and some adyinced koppies in front close to the river. Two companies Staffordshire and two guns being left under Colonel Alleyne to hold the enemy in front, we marched with six companies Staffordshire, and six companies Black Watch round the high range of hills, entirely turning the enemy's position, which we attacked from the rear. The enemy's numbors were not great, bat their position was exteemely strong an,l difficult of access, and they fought with most determined bravery. The Black Watch advanced over rocks and broken ground upon the koppirs, and after having by their fire in the coolest manner driven off a rush of the enemy, stormed the posi- tion under a heavy fire. General &Ile was among the foremost in this attack, and to the deep sorrow of every officer and man in the force was killed on the summit of the koppy. The Staffordshire attacked the high ridge, and over the most difficult ground it was possible for troops to advance upon carried the position. In this attack their gallant commanding officer, Lientenant Colonel Eyre, was killed. Meanwhile the equadrou 19th Hussars, under Colonel Bader, swept round to the rear and captured the enemy's camp. Our success is complete. We bare cap- tured ten standards, and the whole of the position is in ear hands. It is difficult to estimate the enemy's loss, but their dead are lying thick among the racks and in the open, where, when thee l found themselves snrrounded, they tried to rush through our troops. Scarcely any can have es- caped.

." Our own loss is as follows :—Major-General Earle; Lieutenant-Col net Eyre, South Staffordshire ; Brevet Lieutenant-Colonel Coveny, Royal Highlinders ; one corporal and three privates RoYal Highlanders ; three privates South Staffordshire; and two Egyptian camel corps missing; one private Royal Highlanders wounded very severely ; Brevet Lieutenant-Colonel Wauchope, Royal Highlanders, severely woundtd ; Captain Horsburgh, Staf- fordshire, Lieutenant the Honourable J G It Colkorne, Staffordshire, and Lieutenant T Kennedy, Royal High- landers, wounded. Twenty non-commissioned officers and men Staffordshire and 18 Black Watch. List will follow, with written report by special messenger. "Prisoners report enemy I,d by MOUSBI Wad Abuhrzel, Ali Wad Aussein, and Hamid Wad Lekalik. All these are reported killed. The enemy is said to have consisted of the Monassir, with some Rohatab and a force of dervishes from Berber. Our advance by river will he continued to morrow at daylight, and I shall endeavour to carry out your in. structions to General Earle, with which I am fully ac- quainted " "Dalka Island is about 70 miles above Merawi. The attack was well planned and gaPantly executed, and I expect its effect will be to open the way without further fighting to Berber."

GENERAL EARLE OF WARRINGTON EX TRACTION. The late General William Earle is a descendant of an old Lancashire family, settled in Warrington ab mt 1540, and continued resident there up to the end of 1600. Ono ancestor, Rev. Peter Earle born in 1680, was a graduate and Fellow of Brasenose Earle, Oxford, and for some years rector of Grappenhall, Cheshire. Another ancestor, 'John Earle, settled in Liverpool at an early age, was ad- mitted a member of the Corporation of that town in 1703, and was Mayor of Liverpool in 1709. The last-named, among other children, had a daughter. Sarah, married to the Hon. John Stanley, rector successively of Liverpool, Bury, and Winwick, brother of the eleventh Earl of Derby, and a son, William, who married Mrs. Winstanley, of Liverpool, I whose son Thomas, of Spekelands (Mayor of Liverpool, 1 1787), had a son (the fourth), Hardman Earle (born 1792), a well-known Liberal, an old friend of the present Premier and the late 'Mr. J. C. Ewart, for several years prominently con- nected with the London and North-Western Railway Company, who was created a baronet 3rd November, 1869. The late General was the third son of the before-named Sir Hardman Earle, by his wife, Mary, second daushter at the late Mr. William Langton, of Kirkham, near Preston, and consequently distantly connected with the Ilkley family, of Kirkham, Preston, and Manchester. Among his military ancestors may be mentioned Lieutenant-Colonel William Earle, colonel of the 2nd battalion, or Liverpool Fusiliere, one of the Liverpool volunteer regiments raised in 1803 in response to the King's message to the House of Commons to support him in resistance to the extensive military and naval preparations going on in France. The General was born, we believe, at his father's then residence, 36, Hope- street, Liverpool, on May 18th, 1833, so that he was in his 52nd year at the time of his untimely end:---notably, the same age as his distinguished chief in the Soudan, Lord Welseley. He was educated at Harrow, and entered the army as cornet; second lieutenant, 17th Octobar, 1851 ; made lieutenant 6th June 1854 •, captain, 16th February, 1855; lieutenant-colonel, 28th April, 1863;. colonel, 20th May, 1870; and major-general, 31st October, 1880. The General served with considerable dis- tinction in the Crimea at Alma, Inkermann, and Sebastopol, for which he received sth class Medjidie ; was military sec- retary to the Governor-General of India from 1872 until 1876; brigadier-general in expeditionary force to Egypt, 1882, for which he received 2nd class Medjidie. He was married 21st July, 1834, to Mary, second daughter of General Sir William John Codrington, formerly governor of Gibraltar, and leaves issue, two daughters. Lancashire men may well deplore the fate of the brave hero, whose ancestor—John Earle—sprung intro prominence from an ironmonger's shop, which he kept in Castle-street, Liverpool, early in the last century. The most profound and widespread regret was felt at Liverpool on Thursday when the news of the death of General Earle reached that city, and the flag at the Town Hall was hoisted halt-mast high out of respect to the de- ceased and his family. On 'Change the death of the gal- lant General was the absorbing topic of conversation during the greater part of the day. Both General Earle's brothers Sir Thomas and Mt. Arthur—are prominent Liverpool mer- chants, and many expressions of sympathy were tendered to these gentlemen. It is understood that Major-General Brackenburg will push forward with all speed in order to take advantage of the success of Gen. Earle's force. It is probable that the ' command of the brigade will be given to Sir Evelyn Wood, who is next in command in Egypt, Sir Redvers Buller hav- ing joined Sir Herbert Stewart's force at Gubat. WAR CORRESPONDENTS WOUNDED AND MISSING. Reuter's correspondent with General Earle's column was very severely wounded in the engagement opposite Dulka Island. A Renter's telegram, dated Korti, Wednesday, says:—Captain W. H. Gordon, of the Royal Welsh Fus- ilier, who acted as Reuter's corresponchnt during the early stages of the campaign, and latterly as correspondent of the Manchester Guardian, is missing. He was last seen on January 16th alone in the desert, twenty miles from Korn, by an officer, and was put in the direction of Gandul Wells, but since then he has not been heard of. THE QUEEN AND THE NEWS OF THE BATTLE. The following official communication was issued on Thursday :—The Queen was informed this morning of the victory at Dulka, and, while rejoicing at the gallantry dis- played by her troops in storming the enemy's position' her Majesty deeply laments the loss of Major-General Earle and the other officers and men wko fell in the engagement.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 14, 1885.

THE question of Free Schools is likely ere long to become one of practical politics. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN referred to the matter at Ipswich as one of those problems which would have to be solved by the next Parlia- ment. He did not go into details as to his own views on the question, but he let it be known, as he has done on previous occasions, that he is in favour of doing away altogether with school pence in our elementary schools, and thus securing to the people the boon of Free Education. Mr. JESSE COLLINGS, the popular member for Ipswich, speaking at the same meeting, dealt with the question at some length; and, though he is not a Cabinet Minister, his opinions are worthy of consi- deration as those of a thoughtful politician who has devoted himself to this and kindred subjects. Mr. COLLINGS, as is well known, is a bosom friend of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, and it is not therefore at all improbable that they are pretty well agreed as to the course to be taken in seeking to establish a system of Free Schools. The bare thought of the large sum that, it will be imagined, would be required to do away with school pence is sufficient to cause many people to dismiss the proposal as , a luxury beyond reach; but Mr. COLLINGS makes light of this side of the question, and we quite agree with him, at any rate, in think- ing that the cost need be no great difficulty. So far as sabvention from local rates is concerned, he would leave that, as it is, in the hands of the various School Boards through- out the country. His estimate is that, at the cost of a million and a half or two millions per annum, we might get rid altogether of school fees, and he would have the amount provided by the Government out of the Imperial purse—just as the three millions of grant to schools is provided at the present time. He would not leave it, of course, to voluntary managers to deal with this money; Free Schools would really mean Free Board Schools everywhere, for, says Mr. COLLINGS, " the voluntary schools during the hours of secular instruction, whether it might be for four hours a day or five hours, or what- ever it 'sight be, should be under the full control of the elected School Board." It need hardly be said that a proposal of this' kind would be strenuously resisted by those who combine religious and secular instruction in such a way as to lead them to think that they are inseparable. But it should not be for- gotten that so far as the State is concerned, it has nothing to do with religious teaching; the grant is for secular education pure and simple. The member for Ipswich would not debar religious teaching, and he would meet the difficulty in this way: " Outside the hours of secular instruction, before the school begins, or after it ends, the managers should have full use of their school § to teach theology or any thin- else they choose." "But," he adds. "during school hours, the hours for which the Government pays, and for which rates are raised, the schools should be under the government of a School Board; and what would follow would be that the schoolmasters and teachers in the schools, instead of being servants of and under the control of the voluntary managers, would

be the civil servants of the community an.d responsible only to the School Board." It 15 not to be denied that the scheme proposed has the merit of clearness ; and there can be no question that it would meet with the ap. proval of school teachers. It would at once raise their status as a body, and relieve theta I of the drudgery of cramming catechism into the heads of the children along with "the three R.'s''; for as Board School teachers they could no: be called upon to teach any distinctly! religious doctrine. The scheme, too, as rt seems to us, is one which will be likely tO commend itself to the public—and especiallY to parents who, having too many childrefl,. or too few pence, are often in a strait to provide school fees. Taking the country through, there are thousands, indeed we may say tens of thousands, of children away from school every day in consequence of the difficulty ef providing school fees. There can be nO question that a system of Free Schools would be the means of largely increasing the aver- age attendance at school ; while it would relieve Boards of Guardians, School Boards, and School Attendance Officers of that "world of trouble" which they now have with the children of the poorest of the poor. A word or two now as to the cost. is the scheme going to touch John Bull pocket ? Free Education, in the strictest sense of the term, we cannot have, for if the people do not pay in one way they will be called upon to pay in another. TwentY, years ago, the educationist who prophesied that in 1885 the State would provide half the cost of the education ot every child sent t° a National Elementary School would been looked upon as a crazy enthusiast. that is what we are practically doing to-daYh' In denominational schools, about one-fift' of the cost is met by voluntary subscriptions, and in Board Schools as much, or more, comes out of the rates; so that the amount de' rived from school pence is not a large 'tern" after all. Taking the Government return fer the past year for Voluntary Schools for Engi land and Wales, we find that, while "the toes:, expenditure per child in average attendance , is Li is rolAd, the annual income 11'01 school-pence is us id only, the rest ba)6 met by the Government grant and voluntarY subscriptions. Mr. COLLINGS is IllerefOre right in assuming that a Free School syEterd could be established in this country at,slit extra outlay of two millions per annum. TnaA is not much where so much is involved, if the question of cost were the only coast"' eration we should have no hesitation in sa,r ing that we are within a measurable (10,4 tance of realising the dream of many wise an' good men Free Elementary Education throughout the United Kingdom.

5 WIDNES comes out pretty well in the Mel; tality returns, particularly for a town whic is in bad repute for vapours which at ' destructive of vegetable life. The anrilla report of the Medical Officer of Health sh°W: that the death rate for the past Year is but fraction over 22 in the ',coo—about the average, or a trifle over the average of town , life throughout the kingdom. Measles have, carried off 55 children during the year ; be; there has been no such epidemic as ha' visited other parts of the district. In the last quarter of the year in St. Helens, accord' ing to the return just issued by the REGISTAW GENERAL, there have been no less than 135 victims to measles, bringing the death rate, which would under ordinary circumstanCeg have been no higher than that of Widnes, uP, to 33 per i,OOO. The Medical Officer 0i Health for St. Helens calls attention to the fact that the birth rate for that borough is some 20 per cent above the average of tr country, and remarks, rightly enough, that when an epidemic amongst children does se' in; the Mortality is proportionately large' On the other hand, it should be remarked rhati the fecundity of St. Helens is indicative 0 great vitality, so that if children were taltelal care of they would be likely to live, aa, I thrive, and resist disease. There is nu compulsory notification of infectious dis. eases at St. Helens, but it is now Ptd- , posed, in case of an outbreak, to endeavour t,c; I grapple with the difficulty by securing 11s:14 lof cases as speedily as possible. This be good as far as it goes; but it will 11°` be equivalent to compulsory notification:, which is in operation, with good effect, a; Warrington and many other towns. Indeet" SO convinced are the authorities of Warring ton of the advantages of notification 013,s they are extending the system so as t" apply to cases of measles and whoopiei cough. Warrington has also been afflicted( with the measles epidemic, the number deaths for the past quarter from this call; alone being 67 within the borough—Wlll the death rate has risen to 27 in the/ oed; Newton has not escaped, there being IT deaths from measles; but the scourge fr,130 which the Earlestown district has suffereo I, scarlet fever, there having been no less than 3° deaths from this disease during the quarter. It is satisfactory to know that a marked /01; provement has taken place since the las' returns were forwarded to the REGIsTRAIt; GENERAL; the measles epidemic has ettilei run its course, or is being stamped out ; atl; measures are being taken in all the place, we have named for ensuring an improveme°` in the health of the people.

HANDBELL RINGERS AT RUNCORN.—The Royal Poland street Handbell Ringers will give two performances in Run- corn Public Hall on Wednesday next under the auspices of the Runcorn Y.M.C.A. CANTATA AT Itneteonee—Frem an advertisement in our columns it will be seen that a sacred cantata entitled— "Daniel " will be given in Bethesda schoolroom on Tues- day evening next. A very enjoyable performance is ex- pected. BETHESDA MUTUAL APROVEMENT SOClETY.—Themem- bers of this society devoted the meeting on Wednesday evening to impromptu speaking, Mr. Stott's paper on " Re- cognition in Heaven" being postponed until the 4th March. RUNCORN Y.M.C.A. HISTORICAL SOCIETY.—At the fort- nightly meeting of the above society, held on Thursday evening, the Rev. W. Vause delivered an eloquent lecture on "Cromwell, England's uncrowned king." Mr. James Craig, 8.A., presided. RUNCORN STARR•BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—The twentieth appropriation took place in Bethesda schoolroom on Wednesday evening, Mr. Thomas Riley occupying the schair. The ballot resulted in Mr. Samuel Salter, of Elles- mere Port, being entitled to £2OO for twelve and a half years free of interest. HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—At the weekly meeting of this society, held on Monday evening at the Trinity Wesleyan School-room, the following gave readings and recitations, viz. :—Messrs W Rowe, W Moors, W Cook, J T Hughes, R Hughes, W Parry, Miss A Lightfoot, and Rev S Mees. The President occupied the chair. LECTURE ON GENERA. IS GORDON AT RUNCORN.—On Thursday afternoon the Rev. Thomas Evans preached to a fair congregation in Si. John's Presbyterian Church, Run- corn. In the evening, in the some place of worship, the rev, gentleman delivered a lecture on General Gordon. There was a large attendance, and Mr James Handley. IJ.P., presided. RUNCORN AND THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—Mr. R. Shaw, the chairman of the Rencern Improvement Com- missioners, has issued a public notice of his intention to take a poll of the ratepayers as to whether the Ship Canal Bill should be opposed in Parliament by the Commission- ers. The voting papers will be issued on the 24th inst, col- lected on the 28th, and counted on the 2nd March. PRIMITIVE METHODIST BIND OF HOPE, BUNCORN.—Under the presidency of Mr J Ashley, the members of this society gave an entertainment in Regent-street Scheel on Thursday evening. The choir, conducted by Mr Jamm Stubbs, ren- dered selections of music during the evening, Miss Mid. wood presiding at the harmonium. A programme, consist- ing of songs, recitations, dee., was gone through in a creditable manner. Sorts OF TEMPERANCE, Worrole—The "Nil Desperan- dum " division of the above order held their 6th anniver- sary in the Wesleyan schoolroom on Wednesday week, when about 100 persons sat down to a substantial sand- wich tea. After tea Brother Whitehead was celled to the chair, when an excellent programme was gone through consisting of songs, readings, and selections of music ren- dered by the Mill Brow Brass Band. A very enjoyable evening was spent. WIDNES HARRIERS.—A general meeting of this club I was held at the Alexandra Hotel, on Tuesday evening, when it was decided that the dress of the members should be a black jersey and drawers, with illustration of a hare on the back of the jersey, and the motto " fleet of foot" be. neath. The colour of the hare and the motto is to be scar- let, and the stockings and cap to be of the same colour. The club now numbers 70 members, and it If Intended to start a gymnasium on a small scale. SALE OF WORK AT WIDNES.—A "Children's Sole of Work and Christmas Tree" was held at the St. Paul's Mis- sion room, Alforde-street, Widnes, on Monday afternoon, with the object of augmenting the guarantee fund of St Paul's church. The various articles had been collected, and the arrangements made, by the juvenile members of the temperance society in connection with the church, under the direction of Mr and Mrs Thomas, and considerable interest was taken in the event. The proceedings were opened by Mr Neil in a short speech, amongst those present being the Revs J Wright Wil.ions, A P H Wilson, and C Ramat, and Mr jle Iroison, The emount realised by the sale wts £l4. PRESENTATION TO A RCNCORN SCROOLMASTER.—Mr T H Annetehead master of the Holy Trinity Schools,Runeern,has recently been the recipient of a handsome marble timepiece, presented to him by the late choir of Holy Trinity Church as a token of their esteem and regard, and appreciation of the services he had rendered as choir master. Mr. W. Fisher made the presentation in an applopriate speech, in which he referred to the successful labours of Mr. Annett in the day school audio the church, and said he deeply regretted the misunderstanding that had resulted in Mr. Annett ceas- ing to occupy hie usuel place in the gallery after so long a period of service. He had been acquainted with Mr. Annett since he core to Reneorn, and hid always found him to be upright, consistent and gentlemaely in all his dealings.— Mr. Annett, who was unaware of the presentation when he entered the room, replied in a few well•chosen words. Roxanne BURIAL Bose:tn.—The monthly meeting was held at the Offices, Cemetery, on Wednesday. Mr. James Handley, J.P., presided, and there were present 'Ames Moss, Coleburn, Norman, Littler, and S tlkeld (secretary). It was reported that the interments for the ten months end- ing January 25th were 293, corresponding period last year 262, increase 31. The fees received during the same period amounted to £322 12s Id.—Mr. Moss moved the adoption of the Finance Committee's report, which stated that the month's cash account had been examined and found correct, the receipts b?ine, interest en consols £3 lOs 111, fees 1128 94, total X.:11. liars jami. d heen neje wages £9 3s, and the remainder paid into 'blnk. AcCounti amounting to £6 175 Id were recommended for payment. It was also recommended that the tender of Mr. T. S. Carr to clean, wind, and regulate the cemetery clock at £2 per annum be accepted.—Mr. W. Littler seconded the minutes, which were adopted. FIRE AT WIDNES.—Shortly before eleven o'clock on Toesday night Miss Seed, proprietress of the Temperance Hotel, discovered a bedroom on the third storey, occupied and furnished by Miss Wilkinson, confec- tioner, to be on fire. Police-constable Hargreaves quickly spread the alarm, and the fire engine and a supply of hose was quickly on the spot, but only two mem- bers of the fire brigade, Messrs Shepherd and Varley, were on the scene, and some difficulty was experienced in finding the hydrants. There were, however, plenty of voluntary helpers, otherwise the fire might have made some havoc. P.C. Murray ascended a ladder to the room windows and directed a stream of water upon the fitness, which were soon subdued. The whole of the furniture and other property in the Mein were destroyed, the total damage being estimated at above £lOO. The damage to the building is covered by insurance. Valuable help was rendered by Inspector Wood, Sergeants Strickland, and Clarkson, and several constables. Burr ROBBERS AT WIDNES —Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. F. H. GOSsage and Me. H. Gaskell, jun., Joseph Killalea, 14 fifths of coal, value 31, the property of the London and years 3f age, was charged with stealing North-Western Railway Carripeety.—On the morning of the inst P.C. Holbrook saw the prisoner filling a bag with coal which he was taking from a wagon belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company.—lnspector Carter proved that the wagon belonged to the company, and the prisoner was ordered to receive six -ctrokes with the birch rod.--John Randles, 9.5 years Of age, was charged with stealing a cake, volute Id, the property of Edward Allen R )berts, confectioner, Waterlowroad. On the even- ing of the 12. h inst Edward Saye, a foreman engineer re- -siding at 42, Jackson-street, Was passing along Waterloo- 'road when he saw the prisoner enter Roberts' shop, take a cake from the window, and walk away. He stopped him, and gave him into the custody of P. 'C. Thornson.—The prisoner was fined 10s. WIDNES PARISH CHUB= ANNUAL TEA PARTY.— The annual tea party in connection with St Mary's and St Paul's Churches, Widnes, took place on Thursday evening, when about 340 persons sat down to tea. The tables were presi- .ded over by ladies of the congregation. At the subsequent .meeting Mr F Neil (churchwarden), -read a statement of accounts which showed that during the 12 months ending 'the 11th inst, the offertories at St Meey'sChurch amounted 'to £177 15s Id, and at St traul's to £159 15s 61. The ac- counts showed a deficiency of £2l for church expenses. ,Desides the offertories there had been collected from the 'congregation for children's treat £35-„; for temperance brass band £95; eongregetionel tea party last year £18; and various amounts for other objects. (Applause)Mt' Brock, JP, who presided, delivered an address in which he referred to the erection of St. Paul's Church, and urged upon them to free Whom debt as quickly as possible, eulogising the efforts made by the congregation up to the present. He suggested that an organ should be obtained for the edifice, and in conclusion pointed out that the churches had not been built for mere ornament, but for the praise and glory of God. Daring the eveaing songs were giten by Miss White and M. Whorharre .and a duett by Miss Fairley and Mr. J. Fairley. Mr. H. V/. Deacon read Teneyson'a "Revenge," and "Charge of theiLight Brigade." Theeglee class, directed by Mr. Crawford, sang several pieces of music. Mr. J. B. Insison was the accempanist. The usual votes of thanks coach:defi the preceedices. CONCERT AT RUNCGRN.-1 no Mill Brow Brass Bend, on Monday evening, gave a concert in Runcorn Public Hall to a numerous company. Directed by the baton of Mr J Ainsworth, the band performed several pieces of music in a highly creditable style, the audience evincing the hear- tiest appreciation of the efforts of the rising musicians. Miss Williams, of Liverpool, who possesses a soprano voice of a pleasing kind, which she uses with artistic effect, favoured eke audience with an interpretation of the ex- cerpt, "Angels ever bright and fair" and a Welsh ,tnelodys " Taliesins prophecy," and she was heartily recalled on each occasion. Miss Annie Richardson contributed 'Love's old, sweet song" and "To the wood" and although her ' voice appeared to have lost ite old power to char, she eeeceeded in seettring an eneare for her eecand efforde .She then gave a vivacious rendering of "Cherry ripe." Mr Geo Barton had been announced to appear, hut he was absent in conseqeenca ora senere cold. His eon, Mr Geo Barton, jun, proved a worthy suhatitute, singing "Love's request" and "Alice, where art thou ?" in a manner which amply corn. pensated the audienes for the disappointment caused by his father's absence. In response to an encore he sang "The pilgrim of love" with much teethes and power. The comic element in the concert was provided by Mr W Cameron, whose excellent performances were voeiferously encored. Mr R W Pierpoint gave a cornet solo in his usual accompliehed fashion, and Mr Oathwaite was cor- dially recalled for 3 capital performance on the euphonium. Miss Richardson, Miss Rigby, and Miss A Pierpoint acted as accompanists. LINSEED LOZENGES, solklifie4 linseed tea, laxative and de. muloent, 66 postage 21. THE PROPOSED PUBLIC OFFICES AND TOWN HALL —The Clerk read a letter dated the 7th inst. -from the Local Government Board with respect to the application of the Local Board for a provisional order to alter or amend the Widnes Improvement Act, 1867, and the Widnes Local Board Act, 1875, in such a manner as to revive the powers conferred thereby on the Locil Board to construct public offices and a Town Hall, and to borrow money for these pur- poses lot exceeding £25,000. It was also proposed to make further provieion for the borrowing and re-borrowing of such money and for its repayment within a period pre- scribed by the provisional order. The Local Government Board wens prepared to Amend local Acts in the manner proposed, but it would be necessary that the ben-owing of money should , be subject to their sanction, and that the mono/ aso borrowed should be repaid within a period not exceeding 60 years. Before granting their sanction to the proposed lean the Board required to be furnished with de- tailed plans, sections', and estimates of the contemplated works, and ales with areeifications and Lilts of quantities. WHOOPING COLIGH.—There was an attack of this dis- ease during the summer months, happily only one case proved fatal. PUBLIC Wonsts.—A second large contract in connection with the main sewerage of the township has just been com- pleted, and an extension of the sewerage work is contem- plated at an early period. A serious nuisance has been abated by the culverting in a consiierable length of an open sewer which ran near a thickly populated neighbour- hood in the uppsr part of the township. WATER SrPPLY.—The water supply continues pure and abundant. SCAYENGING.—The scavenging was not carried out ID my satifaction during the early part of the year. I, how- ever, represented the matter to my Board, and it is now much more systematic and satisfactory. OFFENSIVE TRADES.—No grave difficulty has arisen in connection with offensive trades. In one instance complaints were made, but the owners of the works complained of have taken means to abate the nuisance, and promised to endea- vour to prevent its recurrence Complaints having been made of the nuisance arising from the waste heaps in this neighbourhood, a correspondence took place between my- Board and the alkali inspectors, which resulted in a confer- ence between a deputation of the Board and the inspectors, when various suggestions for the more careful laying of the waste were made and adopted. In conclusion I may add, on reviewir g the work of the past year 1884, that consider- able progress has been made in carrying cut useful sanitary measures, also that the health department of my Board has devoted itself most assiduously to its often unp;easant duties. . .

CONSERVATIVE , MEETING AT WARIUNGTON. On Tuesday evening a meeting of the Conservatives of the North-West Ward was held in St. Paul's schoolroom, Rolleston•street. Major Litton presided, and there were on the platform. besides others, Sir :Albert Greenall Captain nv.uvultry kor vianam), ana jir. Joist% Roberts. .

The CHAIRMAN, in a few preliminary remarks, said there was every probability—and the probability was much strengthened during the last fortnight through the unhappy business in Egypt—of their having an early election. (liar, h ear.) ) At the same time ha thought t would be a pity for the Conservatives to force the hands of the Government at the present time. They had got the country into a muddle, and it was for them to get us out of it. A ward committee having been elected, Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who was received with ap- plause, raid : Major Litton, Mr. Bottomley, my friends and my acquaintances, lam very glad to be with you on this occasion. We have had these meetings pretty frequently-, they are tolerably numerous, but I don't myself think that under present circumstances they are too frequent. (Bear, hear.) It is very good for me to meet you and learn your views, and it is not an idle business for you to come and meet me, and give me the benefit of your advice, and of your instruction. (Hear, hear.) We know why we cerne to- gether ' • we know the exact (sada of the words gentlemen have just uttered, that one volunteer was .worth many pressed men. (Hear, hear.) Now, Ido desire that we should be united together as a compact body of velem. teers ; that we should not be looking about and desiring to see what an aggregate number of people do, but that we should one and each of us feel that what we do separately and personally ourselves, or ourself, is the real thing and the real guide by which we shall win our battle. (Ap- plause.) Now, gentlemen, I have heard some very good ad- vice, and I have seen some very good practice. The advice was not to make long speeches, and the do,ene right practice was my friends have not made i long speeches. But it s quite impossible new not to refer to one or two subjects. What say von of the condition of Egypt P What say yeu of the cruel and hor- rid war and mortality winch has taken place in Egypt What say you of the forsaking—because he has been for- saken—of as noble a man. of as brave a man, and of as true a man as ever existed ? (Hear, hear.) Is Gordon 6.live ?' e I hope to God he is. (Applause.) If Gordon is a:ive, I hope the country will go forth as on man to rescue him. (Hear, hear.) If gordon should unhappily be a brave man, who has died in the service of his country, I say etnphati cally that Gordon's blood is upon the head of the present administration. (Hear, hear.) Now let there be no mis- taking of our views upon this subject. What I have uttered I have uttered deliberately, and what I have said I firmly believe. (Hear, hear.) And now passing on very quickly, what think you of the condition and state of trade in War- rington ? (Hear, hear, and "It's bad.") What think von of the promises that were mad!, and what think you of the performance of those promise! / Is there one man in thin room who can put his hand in his pocket and say 'if have earned more, lam better off than I was when the preset administration took dffice ? " I am no better, I am worse cff ; I am grievously disappointed, because of the promises that were made have not been fulfilled. I ha ee had the pleasure of meeting Mr. Bottomley before, and I know the little I have said will be well supplemented by Mr Bottomley. If I thought I could utter anything crib fee,_ sandth part as good as I know Mr. Bottomley will utter, I should have gone on speaking to you, but the longer( speak the heavier will be the personal feeling of disappoint- ment that I prevented you frotahearing an eloquent, a welt- instructed and a good than. (applause.) Mr. BOTTOMLEY then addressed the meeting. Referr:rg to Mr. Howes' visit to Warrington, he said that he saw gentleman they had had a gentlem vistlinz tlaern in counectlon with the Liberal party.. Like a pelitizal cornet be (Mr. Howes) visited them at irregular intervals His progress was, like that of most shooting stirs, very erratic indeed. Mr. Howes had spken three nights on different subjec's but not a word had he said in defence of the policy the Government had pursued since it came into power. (Hear, hear.) Having made a few further remarks regardin, HM. owee' lecture!, the speaker went on to criticise at'great length the policy of the Government. Alluding to bid trade, he said he thought it was the duty of either party which might be in power ts, institute an inquiry into the causes of bad trade in order to see what could be done to relieve it. He did not say the Liberal Government was guilty altogether for the distress. (Hear, hear.) He was of opinion that the cause of bad trade was that the pee-. pie of England had to submit to such unr.Or foreign com- petition as they had at the present time. (Applause ) He was not in favour of protecting any one industry at the expense of any other, but he believed in protection all round. If they could not get free trade all round, let them have fair trade. (Applause.) Mr. G. Woons proposed, and Mr. ROBERTS Secon,W, a a vote of thanks to Mr. Bottomley, and a similar vote te the chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: SANITARY CONDITION OF WIDNES.
div.p: THE SANITARY CONDITION OF WIDNES.

At the monthly meeting of Widnes Local Board, on Tues- day, Dr. Cooper, the medical officer of health, presented his annual report for the year ended the 31st December last. It read as follows:—' During this year the number of deaths registered in the township of Widnes was 588, and calcula- ting on a population ef 26,500 persons to the middle of 1884, this gives a death.rate of 22 18 per thousand of popu- lation. The deaths from the seven principal zemotic dis- -eases numbered 124 or 467 per thousand, and were as fol- lows :—Measles 55, scarlatina 5, diptheria 1, whooping cough 1, typhus fever 1, enteric or typhoid fever 11, diarr- ,be of dysentry 50. The deaths of children under one I year (including premature births) numbered 173 or 6.52 per thousand, and of those bstween one and five years 173 or 652 per thousand of population. Tbe grouping into various ages in the following table is in accordance with the tables furnished by the Local Government Board, which are duly filled and accompany this report. Deaths of person under 1 year, 173 ; over 1 and under 5, 173 ; over 5 and under 15, 38 ; over 15 and under 25, 15 ; over 25 and under 60, 126: over 60, 63. The birth during 1884 numbered 1,074, giving a birth-rate of 40 52 per thousand of pnpulatign. 'nifty inquests were held during the year. I will now refer briefly to the outbreak of zymotic diseases which took place during 1884, and the steps taken to arrest the spread of such diseases.

8241.1.1. Pox.—ln the month of June I was called in to see a young woman suffering from small pox. I found, on inquiry, that she had just come from a put of Liverpool where the disease was then prevalent. I reported the case to the Health Committee of my Board, who, in compliance with the request of the patient's mother, decided to send her hack without delay to her home la Liverpool, of course, taking every precaution that neither the patient herself nor the public should suffer by Ler removal. The house .in which the young woman had been staying, and everything with which she had been in contact, were thoroughly disin- fected, the children in the house re-vaccinated. ..Vc. Not- withstanding these precautions, the master of the house I took the small pox; he, however, made a good recovery, 1 and no further case occurred.

MEaSLES.—An outbreak of measles took place in May, and continued until September. It was not confined to any particular district of the township, nor could I discover any special cause for the outbreak. Its long duration lcmsider to be due to the impossibility of keeping children suffering from the disease apart from their friends and scbool•fellows.

's TYPHOID FEVER.—There were eleven fatal cases of typhoid or enteric fever during 1894. These were not con- fined to any special district nor any particular period of the year. In some instances the drainage of the houses where cases occurred were found defective, and disinfection and other remedial measures were promptly applied. • DIAREWEL—Daring the months of July and August, , when the weather was unusually hot this year, many in- fants and very young children fell victims to diarrhcea ;

CABIDEIAN.—The first meeting of the Earlestown and Cambrian (Liverpool) teams at Earlestewn on Saturday afternoon excited a keen interest throughout the neighbourhood. The fact that the Cambrians a fortnight previous bad defeated Everton (the district cupholders) by four goals to three, and as it is extremely probable Earles- town will have to meet the latter in the final tie of the curt competition, caused the match to be looked upon as a teit of tne chances of the Earlestown Club winning the trophy. There was a large attendance of spectators, who were rewarded by witnessing a well-contested game from start to finish. The visitors were, however, overplayed by their opponent, who had their ;nil cup team and were In good form. Having won the toss, the Earleetown captain , selected mu play uplilll,ll,l e;ti., tee eerie re ehc drsu nail. Shortly after the game bad commenced it was evident that the home team had the advantage, and after the lapse of a few moments they began a continual attack on the visitors' goal. At half time the score stood—Earlestown, three goals and two disputed goals; Cambrian, none. On the change of ends the home eleven again pressed their op- penents, and the latter could not make the least headway. When time was called, the Earleatown team had secured a capital victory by five goals to none. LOWTON 17. PAGEFIELD (WIGAN).— The meeting of these old rival teams on the Claiborne Cricket-field, on Saturday, drew an enormous crowd, the spectators being composed of visitor. from Wigan and Lowton, in addition to some hundreds from Golborne and the surrounding dis- trict. Great interest centred on the event, which was for the benefit of W Laybourne, a late member of the Golborne Football Club, who has lost a leg' as the result of an acci- dent at a neighbouriag colliery. .The takings at the gate fully realieed the expectations of the promoters. Pagefield were early in the field, and as their opponents made their appearance party feeling began to make itself apparent, each side having many supporters. Pagefield made a determined attack in the Lowton quarters, but scoring was prevented. From this play was pretty evenly divided, midfield scrim- mages being the order of the day. The next move was a bold dash by Winstanley, who obtained the first try for Pagefield. This was beautifully converted into a goal by Whittaker, amidst loud cheers. Half-time was shortly called, when a dispute arose, which for a time threatened 1 to put an end to the game. Lowton contended that they bad played with fourteen men with the exception of about two minutes from the start, and they now sought to play a new corner. Pagefield objected to this, and as the referee (51r Councillor Hihhert, of Chorley) counted fifteen at the start, the objection was upheld. Lowton failed to find the man they said had dropped out, and they had, therefore, to play the second half with fourteen men. Notwithstanding this, they played up pleckily ; but Pagefield proved too many ror them, Thorpe Kicking a beautiful goal, dropped from the field, shortly after restarting. Pagefield thus won by two goals and one dead ball to nil.

NOTES BY THE WAY. The match between Lancashire and Ayrshire at Deep- dale, on Saturday, was witnessed by about 5,000 spectators and produced some fine play. Both teams were thoroughly representative, and the score may be taken as showing the relative strengths of the two sides. At the start, Lanca- shire seemed to be the weaker of the two, but as the game progressed and they began to understand each otter, this was altogether changed. At the close Lancashire were de- clared victorious by five goals to two. The sub-committee appointed by the British Football Association have met this week, and a number of proposals I were agreed upon respecting the question of prohssionalisrn in football, which will be submitted to the general meeting lof the English Football Association to be hell in London next month. Since the meeting in London on the 18th January, some of the Midiand clubs are coming to the con- clusion-that professionalism ought to be recognised. Judg- ing from this and expressions of a similar nature from other parts of the country, there can be but little doubt the matter will be settled in each a manner as will be conducive te the true interests of the game.

ileMilten is able to exact a lion's share of wha.... e pr, paid miners of Lanarkshire bring from the bowels of the earth by laborious toil; and the American Winans, can depopulate a province that he may enjoy the pleasures of deer-stalking. The more the question is looked into the , clearer does it become that monoply is the fruitful cause of all the evils complained of in connection with the land. To get a vivid conception of how it operate?, let us take a local illustration. Suppose that a century ago the land upon which Warrington , stands, and that in its immediate neighbourhood belonged to a fiftieth part of the inhabitants. Population increases, and invention and science continually facilitate the produc- tion of wealth, until what could formerly not be produced by half a &zeta men, can now be produced by one. It might be supposed that under these circumstances the means of livelihood of the people would increase in pro- , portion to the effectiveness of their labour. And no it I would if land had not been essential to the carrying on of all the affairs of life. But land is essential, and, unfortu- nately, it belongs to but n fiftieth Dart of the inhabltiints;l Th.. ',yule wourd be that the other forty-nine parte, the I landless portion of the community, would compete against each other for the possession of that which was essential to , the carrying on of their business, and even to their very ' existence. If at any particular site in the locality, say On • the batiks of the river or by the side of a railway, material I could be produced and despatched at half the cost which was necessary at some lees favoured site, the saving would clearly be due to the site, and would be demanded by the I landlord. It the producer would not hand it over, then the landlord would eject him from his favoured position and accept some other tenant who would. Were the pra- ducer in aMe like this also the owner of the land be would of course get the whole benefit ef his advantageous position himself, Mat that would not at all benefit the bulk of the inhabitants or of the workmen employed, because the workmen would get no more than the current wages, and the material would still be sold at the market price. During the same period how much more valuable would a shop be- , come which was Situate in the centre of the growing population. This increased value would be given not by any difference in the shop itself, for that might remain ex- actly the same, but by the mere growth of population ' around the site upon which it stood. The additional value would be given Icy the community but enjoyed by the land- lord, simply because lard is a monopoly, and two or more shops cannot be built upon one site. Look at land in town or country, and from whatever point we may, and it is seen to be a monopoly which gives the power to a few to tax the I labour of the many, and the larger the population and the greater the wealth ef a country the more exorbitant is the tax exacted. From considerations such as these it be- I comes clear that the elector who wishes to see a thorough I land reform, but who is perplexed by the multitude of pro- posed remedies, must set himself the question "which of these remedies will most powerfully tend to give back to the I community that put of the value of land which is given to land by the community." Or, in other words, "Which is the remedy that is likeliest to transfer the monopoly of land from the hands of a cllss to the hands of the whole nation ? " The schorne which will most nearly fulfil the requirements ot these questions will be the best kind of land reform.

It might not be unprefit Aile to apply the test here laid down to a few of the principal schemes ot land reform which seem to find most favour. For the sake of brevity I will confine myself to three—free trade ip land, peasant proprietary, and nationalisation of the land. The restrictions on the transfer of land, say the advocates of the first-named of these schemes, is a great cause of the evils of our land system. Let these restrictions be taken away, and the large over-grown, estates will be broken up, farmers and occupiers will become the owners of the land they cultivate, the influx of the agricultural labourers into the town will cease, and the "magic of ownership" will make what is now, so to speak, a desert blossom like the roes. Not a word is said about what is to become of the "unearned increment" which accrues upon land through the growth of the community. That, we suppose, will still go to the owner of the land, and consequently after all these things] had happened land-owning would still be a class monopoly. At the difference would be that the monopo- lists would be more numerous than they formerly were, though still a small proportion of the nation. But, further, we may well ask the champions of free trade in land by what process of reasoning they come to the con- c'usion that their proposals will bring about the things they anticipate. Their theory is that an easy transfer of land will conduce to the breaking up of large estates, but a theory, no matter how pretty or comforting it may be, is not worth a fig if not verifiable by facts. Where are the facts to veirify this theory ? A viry little experience of rural districts teaches that instead ofthere being a tendency to the breaking of large estates into small ones the tendency is all the other way. Work was the law by which they developed their physical organism and mental faculties, and by which their spiritual natures became more godly. Al .zy fellow was a subject of contempt, but there were some who despised la- bour, not because they were laze, but because they believed labour was a degradation. But the fact was that any kind of toil which contributed to the good, convenience, comfort, and ease of society was not a subject to bring disgrace or dishonour to anyone, but rather to contribute to a man's glory and riignity. (Applause.) Some men were everlast- ingly grumlling, arid would make the brightest day in June as sad as the darkest day in November, and they had a horrid power of converting an unquestionable good into a supposed evil. Happiness consisted in the exercise of the social affections. Men were made to be married, and so were women too. (Laughter.) He ,I,is not spin zto say ti•st every man ought to get married, but he knew every women would like to do. (Renewed laughter and applause) God did not intend man to be alone, and there were certain points in his nature which could not be brought out unless be got married. There Was that in the woman which man w ante+, and there was that in the man which woman wanted. Woman wanted man's courage, man's defence, and they would find that the truest and highest type of woman were the better prepared and most readily prepared to link them-. selves to true men. A man would be happy by the exercise Of the faculties of his body as well as those of his mind, and God had put into them elements that sought manifestation in sport. Much of the common melancholy that marked some natures was the result of the lack of physical activity. Man wanted physical activity, and If it was not extravagant it would contribute to the health of the organism, and through that organism, it would con- tribute more or less to the spirit itself, to which it Was closely allied. Happiness depended to some extent on the cultivation of the mind, and no person could cultivate the mental part of their being without becoming richer in en- joyment as well as richer in power. Happiness, too, depen- ded upon a living and abiding fellowship with God. In concluding, the Lecturer observed that all men desired to be happy no matter what their position or possessions might be. Everything ip nature that had life was intended to be capacitated for enjoyment. but some men went to wrong sources for the purpose of securing pleasure. Same people looked upon the world as a place where there was no en- joyment; and man's happiness did not altogether consist in what was outside, but rather within himself. If a man was right within himself he derived happiness from the grand world in which he lived and the universe whick was out- side. (Applause.) At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Lecturer.
