Following the part-song, "Song of the Gipsy Maidens," Miss Wood was encbred for her fine rendering of " Surely." and a similar compliment was also accorded to Mr. Howard, whose clear tenor voice was beard to advantage in "Thou art so near and yet so far." The programme was brought to a eose with the glee, "The Crusaders," and the proceed- ings concluded about half-past ten.

BIGAMY AT PRBSCOT,— At the Liverpool Ass'zes, on Saturday,Jauses Wainwright, 27, labourer, pleaded guilty to having bigamously married Julia Melia, at Prescot, on the 27th April. He was sentezcsd to five years' penal servitude. _ _ _

TEMPERANCE MEETING.—The usual fortnightly meeting of the Church of England Temperance Seciety was held in the Houghton-street schoolroom on Monday evening. The Vicar (ReviH. A. Macnaghton) presided, and the large audi- ence thoroughly appreciated the programme which was given by the members of the Huvton branch of the society. RURAL SANITARY AIITITORITY.—Tne Prescot Rural Sani- tary Authority held a meeting at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon ; present : Messrs W A Meadows (in the chair), W Tyrer, J T Hall, W Newsome, W Ken- wright, E Syder, and S FL Hartley (clerk.)—The minutes ' of last meeting were read and confirmed Medical Officer's Report: Dr F. F Hall (medical officer) reported , that during the month of January the health had been most favourable. No death had occurred front any infec- tious disease, and he had nothing new to report. The death in the townships during the month was : Button 3.5 per 1,000 of the population, Eccleston 25, Hale 3'5, Halewood 1.5, Knowsley 48, Rainhill 0.9. There was no deaths in Bold, Cronton, Speke, Tarbock, Whiston, and Windle.—The Chairman remarked that the report was of a very satisfac- tory character. ..Fxrveyor's Report: Mr John Twist (surveyor) reported that an old standing nuisance in Knowsley-road, Eccleston, was quite offensive, and would be more so as the weather became warmer unless some ar- rangement could be natcle to remove the sewage and fill up the cesspools. The owners of the property near Portico and at Seddon's-brow had not yet provided an improved water supply, and second notices ought to be issued if the Authority purposed doing the work themselves. The income from the sale 'of water would not yield the ten per cent, on the outhy required by the Corporation of St. Helens. The London and North-Western Railway Companrhad written for a water certificate for the stationmastet's Louse at lialeb ink. At the present time the water supply was from a well on the prem:ses, but it was intended shortly to bring water from Ditton through mains belongirg to the company.— Mr Newsome reinirked that the property at Portico was in a wretched state for the want of water, and he thought the occupiers ought to have • a supply.—The Clerk stated that the property owners had agreed to combine and obtain a supply.—The Sewerage Scheme for Ecaeston : The Clerk observed that he had received numerous offers from negoti- ators of loans for the purpose of advancing £5,000 for sew- erage works in Eccleston.—The Chairman : I see that the Sc Helens Corporation are pressing their objection to the Local Government Board.—Mr Newsome : I presume you don't intend to borrow £5,000 at once 7—The Clerk Oh no. That is for the Authority. I should think that the Authority are not likely ts ask for more than £l,OOO for some years.—Mr Hall did not think £l,OOO would do the work they intended to go an with.—The matter then drop- ped, and as this was the only business the meeting con- cluded.

NEWTON COMMISSIONERS. EXTRAORDINARY MEETING. The monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Corn- missioners was held, by adjournment, at the Tdeen Hall, Newton, on Monday afternoon, when there were present, Mmsrs T. J. Gillespie (in the chair), Geo. McCeequodale, J. E. Pardey, J. W. Emmett, T. Stone, J. Fairclougb, T. Forster, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), R. Brierley (surveyor), and Dr. J. W. Watkins (medical officer of health).—The first business was the consideration of the annual report of the medicel officer of health, whiCh was read by Dr. Watkins. It stated that during the year 1331 there were registered, births, 217 males, 227 females; total 444: deaths, 119 males, 112 females ; total 231 : the excess of births being 98 males, 115 females; total 213. The birth rate was 13.09, and the death rate 20 13 per thousand of the population. Appended were tables showing the distribution of the recent epidemic of scarlet fever. During the firet half of the year health was remarkably good. There was not a single case of scarlet fever notified until the 30th June. Then the dis- ease spread steadily until it became epidemic, in November and December. He had male personal enquiries but had completely failed to trace the origin of the infection to I personal communication. The general belief, in wbith he shared, was that the disease was imported at th6:races at Newton Common, bue there was no absolute proof. The fact remained net the township was entirely free before the races, and within a few weeks afterwards the disease broke out. The epidemic was of a bad type, and measles had also been very prevalent. The water supply of the district was excellent in quality, and as he had received no complaints, sufficient in quantity.—Mr. Paracy asked what steps Dr. Watkiks had taken to ascertain the quality of the water. How often bad it been analysed 7—Dr. Watkins replied that he had not analysed it at all.--Colonel Geo. McCorgundale thought the report was a very satisfactory one.—Mr. Pardey: You assume that because the first case of fever appeared after the races that it must necessarily have been imported then P—Dr. Watkins said he did not allege that but be shared in the general belief.—Mr. Pardee, : If it happened to be after a Church Congress you would aseume it was im- ported by the Congress P—Dr. Watkins replied that be would under the same conditions. He weuld Shut up churches as well as schools if he to sweeping measures. Mr. Pardey : Then your only ground is that it happened about the same time 7—Dr. Watkins: It may be only a co- incidence.—On the motion of Mr. Pardey, seconded by Mr. Fairclough, the report was referred to the Sanitary Corn-

------ farmers and small capitalists front buying land. Remove these, it is . said, and small properties will come into ex- istence like mushrooms. It would be as sensible to tell us that were the rocks and cataracts which retard the even current of the Nile cut away the river would reverse its course and flow towards the equator. The tendency to aggregation and combination in all departments of produc- tion and distribution manifests itself in every civilised community. To struggle again& it would simply be not to accept one of those industrial economies which make labour more effFctive. To facilitate the transfer of land would be to take away something which counteracts to some extent the tendency to the nccumulation of land in a few hands. It appears, therefore, that the scheme of free trade M land will not only not accomplish what its advocates desire, but have a directly opposite effect ; besides which it will do absolutely nothing towards taking a monopoly from the control of a case and putting it under the control of the nation.

LEGAL FACT.—The blandekt counsk.l may be a eross- emanniner. Why is the North Pole like an illicit whiskey-manufac- tory ?—Because it is a secret still. A little girl objected to being an angel because she then would have to give up all her pretty playthings and 1.1-4.3 dresses, to wear feathers like a hen. GIIANDPA.—A little boy of six, years was sent one morn- ing to call his grandfather to breakfast. The old gentleman. snored hard, and, as the little boy pushed open the door, he was frightened at the unusual noise. He rushed back to his mother, exclaiming, "Mamma, grandpa has been barking at me! " "You can do anything if you have patience," said an old uncle, who had made a fortune, to his nephew, who had nearly spent one. "Water may be carried in a sieve, if you only wait." " How long ?" asked the penitent spend- thrift. " Till it freezes," was the cold reply. A critic dropped into a studio in Paris one day, stopped before the-portrait of a lady on an easel, and remarked, "It a very nicely painted; bat why did you take such an ugly , model ?" "It is my mother," calmly replied the artist. , "Oh, pardon a thousand times !" said the critic, in great confusion. "You are right ; I ought to have perceived it it resembles you exactly." HOME-CRARITIES.—" Madam," he began, as he lifted his hat at the front door, "I am soliciting for home-charities. We have hundreds of poor, ragged, and vicious children like those at your gate, and our object- is " "Sir, those , are my own children!" she interrupted ; and the front door • I was violently slammed. I - .

- fidIINDED SLANGT.—" Oh, mamma, didn't you tell me that saying 'kid,' instead of child, was slang ?" "Yes, pet." " Welt, just now you was telling about gipsies that steal children, and you talked slang then." "Indeed ! Why, what did I say ?" " You called them ' kid-nabbers.'" A grand jury in ths county ,of Tipperary once passed the following resolutions:--" Resolved : That the present gaol is insufficient, and that another ought to be built. Resolved: That the materials of the old gaol be employed in construct- ing the new one. Resolved: That the ohl gaol shall not be taken down until the new one is finished." One day opposing pickets on the Rappahannock, during the war between North and South in the United States, agreed not to fire. A brisk conversation arose between a Texan and an Irishman on the Federal side. " What are you doing in the Yankee army ? What are you fighting for, anyhow ?" said the Texan. "I'm a-ilghtin' for thirteen dollars a month; I belave you're a-fightin' for eleven dollars," answered Pat.

_ A funny story is told by a contemporary of the sexcen- tenary of Merton College' Oxford, which happened some twenty years ago. A Fellow of Merton at that time, known to his friends as Curius Deotatus, used to write leading- articles for one of the chief London journals. He wrote one in advance on the Merton sexcentenary, describing it as a magnificent success; and then went down to take his part in the festivities. To his horror, and to the disgust of the pro- prietors of the journal in que,tion, the article appeared on the morning of the anniversary, and the number of old Mer- ton men who were coming up from all parts of the country, seeing the elaborate lucubration, concluded that the affair was over, and stopped at home. How lIE FELT.--at the battle of Antietam, during the 1 Civil War in America, a company,of soldiers were ordered to a field a little distance from the lines. It wan not ex • peeled that there would be any work for them to perform, and the captain's servant, a stalwart darkey called Sandy, ; accompanied them to their new position; hut hardly had they got there when the balls began to fly around like hail, wounding the captain and cutting up the men. After the I captain had got to the hospital and the servant had ben found, the captain questioned him as to where he was during the fight " Well," said Sandy, "I thought it war gettin' ruder too hot for me, mama, an', seem' a big tree on tie ; ground, I laid down behind it, so dey couldn't hit me." 1" Bow did you feel lying there ?" asked the captain. "1 I just felt, massa, as if ebery hair ob my head was a brass band, an' ebery band playin" Home, sweet home I'" Artemis Ward had a poorly-painted pinorarna. When anything especially bad appeared, he would look admiringly at it, and then, with a look of reproach at the audience, remark, "Tins picture is a great work of art. It is an oil- painting done in petroleum. Ills by the old masters. It was the last they did before dying. They did this, and then expired. I wish you were nearer, so that yen could see it better. I wish I could take it to your residences and let you I see it by daylight. Some of the greatest artists come here I every morning before dayrght with lanterns to look at it. I They say they never saw anything like it before, and hope they never will Ifagain " Then, pointing to some vile splashes o paint •: , "These are intended for horses. I know they are, because the artist told me so. After two years he came to ' me and said, 'Mr. Ward, I cannot conceal it from you any longer. They are horses.'" LITERAL OBEDIENCE.— Dr. Boyer, one of Coleridge's teachers' had an antipathy to nicknames, and had been annoyed because the boys would persist in calling one Simon Jennings, an unpopular student and a clergyman's son," Pontius Pilate." He ordered them sternly never to say "Pontius Pilate," but always "Simon Jennings," or they would suffer for it. One day a class was reciting the Catechism. The Apostles' Creed fell to a boy noted for his (dulness. He droned along carelessly to "suffered under," and was about to add " Pontius Pilate," when suddenly the threat of the master and the sure penalty flashed on him. Thankful that his memory had served him so well, he added with energy "under Birdon Jennings, and was crucified." Down came the merciless cane of Dr. Boyer on head and shoulders; and veh.-, illla nreatri he cried in anger " What do you mean, sir ?" The boy, astounded at the sudden flogging, said crustily, "You ordered us, air, always to say 'Simon Jennings' instead of ' Pontius Pilate,' or we should be whipped," and appealed to the class if it was not so. Dr. Boyer was silenced. Jie had flogged the boy for too literal obedience.

THE CUE—APEST OF WIVES —They were spinning yarns. One old man sat apart from the others and looked sad and forlorn, as if he never thought of levity in all his life. "My wife has been one of the cheapest luxuries a man ever en- joyed," said one. "We have been married eighteen years, and she has cost ins less than a thousand dollars all told." "Pooh!" said another. "I have been married nine years and my wife's total expenses have been scarcely three hun- dred dollars." The sad man drew a deep sigh and said : "'Well, well! I was married forty years ago, boys, and from that day to this my wife has cost me only one hundred and nineteen dollars, and she has had everything she needed too." "Row in the world did you get through so cheap ? "The poor gal died the second week after I married her." The crowd spared his life because he was sad. PAT'S DECEPTIOII.—An inside car full of travellers was toiling up one of the long hills in the County Wicklow. The driver leaped down from his seat in front, and walked by the side of the horse. The poor beast toiled elowly and wearily, but the six insides were too busily engaged in con- versation to notice how slowly the car progressed. Presently the driver opened the door at the rear of the car and slammed it to again. The "insides " started, but thought the driver was only assuring himself the door was securely closed. Again the fellow repeated the same action; he opened the door and slammed it to Again. The travellers turned around I angrily, and asked why he disturbed them in that manner. Whisht," whispered the fellow—"don't spake so loud— she'll overhear us !" "Who is she ?" " The mare. Spake low," he continued, putting his hand over his nose and mouth. "Sure, I'm desavin' the crayture ! Every time she hears the door slammin' that way she thinks one of 3ez is gettin' down to walk up the hill, and that rises her sperrits." The insiders took the hint. In a horse-warranty case that was tried before the late Mr. Justice Mauls an important witness was a "horsey "- looking young gentleman whose pert and priggish manner appeared. to produce a by no means favourable impression on the Court. To a question from counsel, "Do you under- stand horses, sir?" he replied, "There are two animals, sir, I consider myself a perfect judge of—a fine horse and"— bowing towards the bench, on which some ladies were seated —"a fine woman." The judge looked at him quietly for a moment or two, and, on the termination of his evidence, as he was about to retire, said, "Stop, sir t 'You have kindly informed the Court you are a perfect judge of two animals— a fine horse and a fine woman. Then take my advice. If you have not yet made your will, do so at once, and insert a clause that after death your hide shall be tanned and made into a side-saddle, and then you will be between the two animals you know most about."

HOIST WITH lIIS OWN PETARD.—A good story is told at the expense of Lord Ellenborough, the celebrated judge. He had to attend the assizes in a neighbouring town, and was about to set out on his journey in the family coach, when his lady begged to be allowed to accompany him. He con- sented on condition that she did not attempt to fill the carriage with parcels as she was fond of doing. When they had proceeded some miles his lordship, in stretching his legs, struck his foot against a box that Lay under the Opposite seat. Believing it contained her ladyship's bonnet, he drew it forth, pulled down the window, and flung the offending article into a ditch. The coach immediately stopped, and the footman got • down. "What are you stopping for, sirrah ?" shouted the judge, "If you please, your lordship, a box has dropped out of the cerriage, and—" "Drive on," bellowed Ellenborough. And the box was left behind. On arrival at his hotel in the town in which the assizsa were about to be held the judge immediately proceeded to robe. When ready he shouted to his servant, "My wig; quick, bring nay wig." "Beg pardon, your lordship," stammered the servant, "but your lordship flung it out of the carriage nto a ditch."

THE STROKE OF Dome—The other day a lady in Paris, baying paid her hotel bill, sent away her boxes on a cab ani sallied forth on foot. No sooner bad she departed than the landlord discovered that the clock had disappeared from the mantelpiece of the room which his late lodger-had been occupyingt though he remembered to have seen it there sub- scqientlyM her trunks being despatched. Convinced Vent she must be the thief, he rushed out in hot pursuit, and, overtaking her, he charged her with the robbery and gave her into custody, the lady meanwhile protesting loudly against the indignity offered her and vowing vengeance ag dint the traducer. She was, however, taken before the juge d'instruction, to whom she resumed her torrent of indig- nant denial with the extraordinary volubility peculiar to the daughters of Gaul. Her indignation was at its height when, b, twelve o'clock rang forth in clear tones from the region of madame's dress-improver! The expression of con- sternation depicted upon the fair pilferer countenrece, together with the appositeness of the quaint phenomenon, were too mnch for the gravity of the officials, who burst into uncontrollable laughter. Five minutes later a female warder returned the tell-tale timepiece to its owner.

It is well kn sten that the Indians were formerly far more successful in the 1-eat- merit of inflammatory disease than the most skilful and learned white men. It has been thus used fir more than half a century, healing the most inveterate diseases, and giving jay and health to vast numbers. Tire power of the Green Mountain Vegetable Oint- ment is astonishiegly great. There is no medseine known that ean surpass it in prompt and energetic action. Applied in suf- ficient quantities to the endwise of the body, in the vicinity of the most highly inflamed parts, wheth-r external or intense), It at once subdues the inflammation and pain. It is peculiariy adapted as a sovereign remedy for the gent, rheumatism, neuralgia white swellings glandular swellings. ague in the face, bronchitis, quinsy, croup, sore throat, erysipelas, inflam 'nation of the eyes, broken breasts, sore nipples, hard tumour,, ringworms, scaldhead, wasp and bee stings and poiso_ ous wounds, chilblains, cholie, inflammation of • the chest and bowels, fistals, boils, piles. scrofulous sores, burns, scalds, bruises, abscesses, fresh cut wounds, and old inveterate ulcers. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

The war la the Soudan has proceeded through stages that certainly lack nothing of the dramatic element. Nearly eyery morning the newspaper reader has served up to him some startling surprise, some vivid picture of hard fought battle. News of the fall of Khartoum was followed by anxiety as to the fate of Sir Charles Wilson. This was promptly followed by his rescue after a gallant dash by Lord Charles Beresford. Then came the anxious controversy as to the possibility of the death of General Gordon. At the front there does not appear any doubt on the subject. Lord Wolseley himself has abstained from a definite statement of belief. That telegrams from the camp report that everyone there believes that Gordon is dead. In England there is a strong indisposition to accept this statement. The reports of Arab scoots, spies, and prisoners have so frequently been proved to be mere inventions that there is hope even against hope that the circumstantial story of Gordon being stabbed at the door of the Government House may yet prove a fiction. The statement published this morning .on the authority of an Italian Colonel who knows Khartoum well. disposes of a point of which much has been made. Waen Sir Charles Wilson neared Khartoum, he found no Egyrian flag anywhere flying. It was argued that if GJraen were alive, whether in the Catholic Mission Church Cr elsewhere, ha would have kept his flag flying or Otherwise made know his presence to the English party. The Italian Colonel says the Catholic Mission House where Gordon is believed to be is not visib'e from the point reached by Sir Charles Wilson. The building is, he testi- fies, very strongly fortified with a large and strong en- trenchment. It is probable that every day for weeks to come will have its rumour about Gordon. Bat we are still permitted the hope that he ruay be found alive. This morning the intense interest in this great war- d:am% was worthily maintained by news of the battle on the Nile, which General Earle won at the expense of his own gallant life. It is only a few days ago I received a letter from an officer in the Grenadier Guards, who, volun- teering for active service, found himself attached to General Earle's command in the dreary toil round the bend of the Nile for Berber. He spoke with pathetic discontent of his position. It seemed that all th 3 fighting and all the glory were reserved for Stewart's division. ",Here we are, he wrote, Wiling along at the rate of six miles a day, doitWdonkey's work rather than soldier's. By the time we reach Berber it will all be over. With Khartoum taken, Gordon rescued, and the Mandi beaten off, it is not likely they will give us even a brush at aaber. These are hard lines after all we have suffered." This letter was, of course, written just after Abu Klea, and before Sir Charles Wilson's expedition down the river to Khartoum. Within a few days all has changed, and this gallant young fellow, who would.seem more at home in a ball-room than on a battle field, has by this Hoes had his fill of fighting. It would be a mistake to suppose that because the efforts to damage the GAvernment have for the moment failed they will not hereafter be renewed in a more systematic fashion. This day week Parliament will meet, and one of the first moves of the Conservative leaders will be to ask for a day on which to discus the policy of the Govern- ment in Egypt. Sir Stafford Northcote has already sounded a note of battle in a circular issued to his supporters in the 1101133 of CJMITIOUI. This is of an un- usually truculent nature, pointing directly to a vote of censure. Lord Salisbury is hastening home, and his circular .to the Peons may be ex- pected. any day. A session which seemed to promise, for the outset at least, a quiet and uneventful time, is now likely te burst forth into flame. There is no chance of the Ministry being left in a minority. Bat the Conservatives Lelleve they can abstract a few votes from Liberal.; of the standard of Mr. Goschen and Mr. Joseph Cowen, which they think am worth fighting for. Mr. Gladstone, I hear, wet- Comes with ardour the opportunity of meeting the indict- ment. .bate irt the House of Commons is a very different thing from speech- eakt,g—in the country, or from articles in party journals. The charge against the Govern- ment was within a few hows of the arrival of the news of Khartoum hysterically named up by an evening journal in the phrase "Too late." That is all very we'l. But what the Conservatives will be obliged to show is that there was in consonance with the whole circumstances any earlier date at which a relief expedition cmald have been der patched.

- Gonservative platform orators and newspapers Mate I with a disingenuousness that is appalling that an expedition to the Soudan is very much like an excursion to the High- lands or a jaunt to the South of France. When would Sir Stafford North cote or Lord Salisbury have had the expedi- tion start? It WAS on the 24th of Marc e that Khartoum was invested, and on the 9:h of April the news reached Lon- don from Gordon, who reported a constant series of success- ful engagements with the enemy. Fad it been other wise and had the necessity for rer,,, imperatively appeared would the Consery itivan have -.rl five or six thousand British soidiers sent out to arrive in the Soudan in the deadliest heats of summer October is regarded as the earliest date, at 'Which British troops could live and work in the climate of tee Seudan. It W 49 in August that the expedition bigro to start, its progress being pushed forward with unrecdtting energy. On the 10:h September Lord Wniaerey anived at Cairo, and even Conservatives will admit that he is rot the man to let the grass grow under his feet. Leaving these shores in the middle of August, the advance guard usier Gc ieral Stewart reached Gubat five months later—on January 13th. It was towards the end of March that the storm first burst round the heads of the Government, and accusations of abandoning Gordon were, as the newspapers of the time show, daily levelled at them. Bearieg in mind the dates mentioned above, it will be seen that in order to have done what their political opponents accused thcm of criminally leaving undone, the Govern- ment would hive had to despatch the rescuing oarty in November, 1833, two months before Gordon himself started. These are simple facts that appeal to common sense and common honesty, and are not to be finally obscured in the smoke of vague accusations. The Little House in Lambeth where Mr. Fawcett spent many years of hard labour, and whither in the end success came to him, 13 in the market "to be let furnished." The neighbourhood 13 not exactly that which a Postmaster General and prospective Cabinet Minister would elect to live in. It lies just over Vauxhall Bridge, within sound of the shriek of the South-Western Railway engines, and in close Proximity to a large gasworks. It is very bad of access from all sides, but once there there arecompeneations to be found. At the back et the house is a large piece of ground which gives the place its name, "The Lawn." The house i.e moderately retired from the front aspect, one of a crescent Of houses shaded by large trees. It also had the other ad- vantage that the rent was low. Mr. Fawcett had the garden etneasured. There was nearly an aerie in all, and round the utmost limits he used to take his daily allowance of measured miles. 01 course he could do this without gaid- &lce or assistance, and walking along at a swinging pace he composed much of his literary work, and when he was go- kg to speak in the House of Commons, thought out his line of argument. Mr. Fawcett was not the kind of man to grow rich, and though he left baldrel him perhaps a larger sum of money than was expected, it is not sufficient to keep a family upon. There was at one time a suggestion to offer Mrs Fawcett the honourable position of principal of Girton College, a poet she would have admirably filled. The thing has, however, fallen through for the present, and in the meanwhile Mre. Fawcett has gone to live with her sister, Miss Agnes Garrett, who, with her late sister Rhoda, established a lucrative business as house decorators. Mrs. Fawcett is a woman of business, and will be of much use in such an establishment. Each of the three living sisters of this family is remakable in her way. Mrs. Fawcet:, was the right-hand man of her husband. She hunted up re- ferences for him, was always ready to assist him in his daily work, and, with his collaberatim, wrote a book on political economy. Miss Garrett is, as already mentioned, at house decorator upon art principles. People who are not certain of their own taste in house furnishing and decorat- ing call in Miss Garrett, give her carte blanche, go away for a term, and return to dud their house in irreproachable form. This is perhaps not tke best way of making a home. But it suits some people, who would be lost or would commit all kinds of anachronisms if left to their own devices. Another sister is Mrs Garrett-Anderson, or as she is sometimes called Dr Garrett-Anderson. She has a very wide practice as a (t)cter, her skill being lees and less grudgingly admitted by the male doctors. Mr. Cross in his" Life cf George Eliot " has for obvious reasons, been more communicative with respect to his wife's Sunday receptions than of any other portion of her home life. These were In a sense public, and may therefore be written of without offence. It struck me in reading this part of the book that the biographer omitted notice of what to a casual visitar was the prevailing feature. To my mind It was the somewhat too effusive awesomeness of the social gathering round the great writer. It was almost like being in church, people when they ven- tured to speak to each other talking in whispers. The completeness of my testimony is limited by the fact that I STU privileged to be there only twice, and this was in the last days of the gathering. On one °cession Ruskin dropped in and there will for ever live in my memory the strauge scene—Ruskin seated on a chair almost knee to knee with Mns Lewes en another, and gathered around a circle of almoet literally gaping admirers. It was a great privilege to hear the convereational give-and-take of these great leaders of thought. But it seemed to me at the time that we might have availed ourselves a little lese obtrusively of the opportunity. A consiaerable proportion of the visitors were ladies, some there evidently for the first time and de- termined at all hazards net to lose one crumb of the intellec- tual barquet. Still it was very funny.

An old minister had occasion to stay at :the 'residence of a brother clergyman, who was an old bachelor. In the morning the host was up and ready for breakfast, but his guest *as about an hour late. The bachelor, wishing to reprove him, remarked that his motto, like the Duke of Wellington's, was "that the first turn should be a turn out.' The minister, with ready wit, replied that his motto was "that one good turn deserves another." KAY'S COMPOUND. a demulcent anodyne, expectorant, for Coughs and Colds. TEETOTALISM IN EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—" Tee Tee" clkd in question my statements about the Jews and of Christ not condemniag their intemperance. I substantiated by giving some of the best living and modern literary authorities. He, when compelled to reply, con- fesses his ignorance and tries to excuse himself by a level- ling down process of your readers ; and would palm this off as serious business. In my last I confuted his erroneous conclusions by quoting from teetotal authorities, men whose opinions deserve some consideration. His reply is that he would b 3 at sea if he ado,4ted them. Quite trite. . . .

--- He mays lam evading .his pertinent points. I am sur- prised at his simplicity in calling these two questions per- tinent. Anyhow I decline to discuss these or any other questions until my second letter is answered. One thing at a time ; but it is quite evident " Tee Tee" is ignorant of the rules of debate.—Yours truly, MODERATOR. PRO EONO PUBLICO, OR PRO BONO PUBLICAN? Sir,—Councillor W. Bolton at the last meeting of the Town Council, was very emphatic in his denunciatkon of Sunday Closing, and scolded the propmer of the petition, in terms more forcible than elegant. I never knew this elo- quent and high-minded Councillor display half the fervour in tha iMerests of the public, which he then showed in the interests of the publican. Now, sir, I think it a question his constituents may well consider whether he is " within his rights" when thus using his position as Councillor to push his own interests, as against the interests of the com- munity; whether the power thus canferred upon him, shall be exerted to frustrate all endeavours to mitigate, if not des- troy, an acknowledged evil. The petition to Parliament in favour of Sunday Closing is such an en4eavour, and opno- sition to it comes with a very bad. grace f rom a Coun- cillor who is also a brewer. Can Mr. Bolton honestly say he believes the continuence of Sunday drinking to be condu- cive te the interests of the community? Does he advocate it as having an elevating tendency? Truly nam are raised to a "bad eminence " by this means ; some even as high as tbegel!ows! I shall look forward to a continuance of this discussion with great interest, in the lave of finding Mr. Bolton em- ploying argument in his cause. Hitherto we have only had vituperation conceived to self-interest, and delivered in bad taste.—l am, do., PRO BONO PUBLIcO.

div.head: ST. BARN tBAS CRURCEI_ TEA PARTY.
div.p: ST. BARN tBAS CRURCEI_ TEA PARTY.

Sir,—lt- will be seen from an advertisement that a tea party is to be held on Tuesday next, in connection with St. Barnabaa Church, and I trust you will grant me this favour- able opportunity of making known through your columns a few important facts concerning this large poor pariah. Since this mass of poor people were cut off from their well-to-do brethren of St. Paul's, they have bad to stand alone and struggle on as best they could, without either sympathy or support being forthcoming from the quarter where it might have been most expected. But all will be glad to hear that their worthy vicar, the Rev. J. Allton, still straggles on among his people to keep pace if possible with the rest of the parishes; and we may tope to see in the result that the hand of sympathy has been extended by ell those who wish such noble efforts as are made in this pariah God I-. Under the most favourable circamstances, there is always an immense amount of mental and physical energy to be expended in a large parish by any faithful and zealous pastor; and a clergyman haviag a good living and a worthy congregation to look back upon will Sod a great deal to cheer and to encourage him in his arduous labeurs. Mr. Allton his neither the one nor the other of these supports; and when we find a man displaying such amount of unselfieh- nes, and straining every nerve for no other reward here than the good of his flock, we must feel that he is deserving ef all the support it is possible to give him. Over 5,000 working people need food, cl )thes, and other commodities useful to life; thus all classes more or less must be benefited by them. At present a vast amount of distress prevails in this part of the town owing to the iron trade being so slack for such a long time; and many families are dependent upon men who have only had six to nine days' work sines Christmas consequently the respectable poor are unable to give anything for church or other work, but require regular assistance themselves. Thus it will be easy to understand how needful it is that every one who can shored give a little, and by their presence try to make every effort that is uudertaken for these people a success while they are without funds, wealthy people, or other aids .ex- cept a hard-working Sim aid hi, family, who with fe few trusty parishioners by to do their best even though it be small. It II to be hoped that those well-to-do parishes in Warrington will add their mites to aid in this good wroth, and thereby prove themselves to be not only "one in hope and doctrine," but also "one in charity" in the true sense of the word. _
Apologcsing for taking up so mush of your valaab!. space, I am, air, yours, &c, A PARISIIIONE%.
MR. NORMAN, SEN., AND ECONOMY AT RUNCORN. _ .

Sir,—At a mseting of --tl-oe.in-n-c-o-rio Commissioners; held some months ago, Mr. Norman is reported to have a iid that he would do all he could to "facilitate the expenses of the Board." Previously to that meeting I had been under the impression that he posed himself before the ratepayers as an economist and friend of the working-man. Looking over the reports of the meetings of two public bodies to which he belongs, the remarks above quoted came forcibly to my mind, as evidently it was no lapsus lingua as it had at first been generally supposed, but a real hard fact. At the 1 last meeting of the School Board I find he advocated the 1 policy of making all the schools in Runcorn Board Schools. "Tarn them all into Board Schools, that's it." Has he I ever thought of the consqquences that would ensue to the! ratepiyers if this were done? The expenditure of the rates 'I would be " facilitated" without a doubt by such a course. 1 Or does he find the schools with which he is somewhat associated an incubus, the management and cost of which he would readily and graciously hand over to the represen- tatives of the ratepayers, providing he were free? A good way of showing sympathy to the poor ratepayers most un- doubtedly! Again, at a recent Commissioners' meeting he advocated four i.nportant offices of that body being filled by one and the same man (of course, providing he could find a man willing to fill this compound office). Surely he did not really intend this; fancy such a jack-of-all-trades having affixcd to some prominent port of his uniform be would not be complete without it—Runcorn Market, Lodging - house, Sanitory, and Scavenging Inspector. Moreover, he could not expect for a single minute that such an officer would be able to do one-tenth of the work without a saddle horse, or other rapid means of conveyance. Therefore I assume this is another schema for facilitating the expenses of the Board. But thee such an important official as he wishes to create might facilitate the expenses in another way. Being sanitary in- spector, he would of necessity have to visit places where an infections diseise might at some time be rampant, and then duty might call him to mix amongst the market people and hucksters. What would prevent such an officer carrying the infection from oafs place to another, and thereby dis- seminating throughout the town one or other of the diseases that already sometimes approach epidemic. Perhaps, how- ever, Mr. Norman's fertile brain and inventive power has prepared a special non-infectious-and-contagious armour for the said inspector. I pity such an officer, and hope; the Commissioners will have the good sense to set themselves firmly against the creation ef such a one, and that the rate- payers will remember this false economist at the next elec.. tion.—l am, sir, yours truly, A RATEPAYER.

div.head: RUIFORN COMMISSIONERS AND THEIR OFFICIALS.
div.p: THE RUIFORN COMMISSIONERS AND THEIR OFFICIALS.

Sir,—l wish to make a few observations with reference to the recnat action of the Commissioners towards their of& cials, as many of the ratepayers are of opinion that the con- duct of the Commissioners is very strange and inconsistent. For instance, they have made an appointment of a stranger to the office of secretary and accountant, which is condemned throughout the town, seeing that there are men who have resided in Runcorn many years who are quite capable of performing the duties. It appears to me strange that they should relieve the secretary's department from a portion of the work (i.e., the collecting, which according to Mr. Nor- man's testimony at a recent meeting is about four months' work each year), and yet give as much salary to the new official as that enjoyed by Mr. Brookes; or, in other words, Mr. Brookes has had 16 months' work a year and anly baen paid for 12 months. Mr. Fisher is reported to have said, "We spent Some hours going through the secretary's duties, and he could assure the Board that they were as- tonished at the multiplicity of the books he bad to keep. It was evident that with the books and the number Of meet- ings the Board were now holding, that there was work enough for one man without kim going outside the place to loik after money." This is either peculiar economy to give a man as much salary for only two-thirds of the work that was performed by his predecessor, or on the other hand Mr. Brookes must have been oonsiderablv underpaid for the valuable work he has done for the Board.

Many of the ratepayers are of opinion they should have retained Mr. Brookes, considering the knowledge and ex- perience he has of the business ef the Board, which I be- lieve extends over a period of eleven years. During that period there has been quite a revolution of the work of the departm,-nt ; a large number of Acts of Parliament affect- ing locil authorities hes been passed, not forgetting the Canal Boats Act, and the adoption of the Public Libraries Acts, of which Mr. Brookes has had considerable experience, and now, forsooth, his services are to be lost to the town. I should like to ask how the Commissioners propose to re- compense him for the extra work he has done. With reference to the appointment of Mr. Barker as col- lector, I think that if anyone will take the trouble to look at the prescribed duties of a surveyor, they will find that with the mileage of streets in the town, and the architec- tural work required of him, there is quite sufficient work Without the collecting. It appears to me that some members of the Beard wish to make themselves popular by grinding down the officials, and if rumour be trae, there is likely to be I a muddle in connection with the appointmentof an Inspeeor of Nuisances, and great changes are to take place in the management Of the mrket. There seems to be a general sifting all ront.d. Where is the reorganisation going to stop ? Will it not affect in some was, the Canal Boat In- spector, the Law Clerk, or Medical Officer ?—roura faith- fully, OBSERVER. ' Runcorn, Feb. 12th, 1885.

The Rev. Stephen Gladstone and Mrs. Gladstone return on Tuesday next to Hawarden from the honeymoon at Halkin Castle. The occasion will be made a general holiday at Hawarden. There was a consultation of Ministers at the Premier's official residence yesterday afternoon. Mr. Gladstone, Lord Granville, Lord Kimberley, Lord Northbrook, and the Marquis of Hartington attended. At a meeting at Exeter on Friday, a resolution, propo- sed by Earl Devon, seconded by a Wesleyan, and supported by a Jew, was unanimously passed in favour of presenting Bishop Temple with a testimonial. THE CLERICAL IMPOSTOR —George Robert Lee, alias Samuel Robv Leigh, aged 28, was convicted at Wolver- hampton, on Friday, of defrauding his landlady of a fort- night's board and lodging, on the pretence that he was a clergyman. He was sentenced to fire years' penal servitude.

Each parent WAS or- dered to have the operation performed in a mouth. These prosecutions are exciting very bitter feelings.

- - DYNAMITE EXPLOSION.—THREE MEN SERIOUSLY INJURED. A tremendous explosion of dynamite occurred on Friday evening in Goragh Wood Quarries, near Newry, by which three men sustained injuries which will Probably prove fatal. The men were engaged in extracting an unexploded dynamite charge when it suddenly exploded with great violence. All were terribly injured and their eyesight destroyed. THE LIBERAL CANDIDATES FOR NORTH-EAST LANCA- surug.—An important meeting of the Executive Committee of the North-East Lancashire Liberal Registration Associa- tion was held at the Manchester Reform Club on Tuesday afternoon, Sir Ughtred Kay-Shuttleworth presiding. Dur- ing the meeting it was reported that the Marquis of Hart- ington had selected the Rossendale district as the cunstitu• else', he will contest at the next election. The selection of Rossendala by Lord Hartington will give great satiefaction to the Liberals of Rossendale Valley, where he is exceed- ingly popular.' As his right-hand- man, he will have Mr. , Thomas Brooke, J.P., of Crawshaw Hall, the present High Sheriff, with whom he has stayed on his previous visits. With such a candidate the Liberals are sure of a victory— indeed, the seat would be regarded as a safe one with a much less pepular.man. The selection of candidates for the other three districts will, of coarse, be left to the several organi- sations. Already the question of candidates has naturally been under discussion, and, though no decision has been arrived at in any of the districts excepting Rossendale, an opinion may be -formed as to probabilities. A correspondent gives the following as the probable list of Liberal candi- dates :—Rossendale. Lord Hartington ; Accrington, Mr. F. W. Grafton; Clitheroe, Sir V. Kay-Shuttieworth ; Damen, Mr. John Gerald Potter.

div.p: BURNED.

A Central NLITS telegram, dated New York, Friday morn- ing, says :—During last night a fire broke out man asylam at Philide!phia. The flames were confined to the male department of the building. The inmates were all of the pauper class. Most of the unfortunate beings had retired to rest when the filmes were first discovered, and their terror when they found thenvelves surrounded by fire was terrible in the extreme. A few sprang from the windows, but the majority were too terrified to make the attempt, and were burnt to deat. The shrieks of the poor victims roused the whole locality, and though strenuous efforts were made to rescue them, it was evident that a large number had perished. The building was gutted, and the fire speedily burnt itself out. The firemen searching among the rains have already recovered nineteen bodies, all being those of lunatic Inmates. It is believed that altogether forty hare perished.
FRIGHTFUL BOILER -EXPLOSION: FIVE PERSONS KILLED.

A disastrous boiler explosion occurred on Friday at Bickenham, Kent, by which five persons were killed and an immense amount of damage done. It occurred at the Mid. Kent Brick Works, which turn out a quarter of a million bricks weekly. The works were going on as usual, when about eleven o'clock a tremendous explosion was heard, and the tall chimney stack fell with a loud crash. A terrible panic arose in the neighbourhood, and apprehensions of another dynamite outrage were rife, but on levestigation it proved that the boiler of the stationary engine had burst, and the building in which it stood was wrecked. Efforts were immediately made to ascertain what injuries had been indicted on the workdeople, and, on searching the ruins, five dead bodies were extricated. Three men, named Edwards, Carter, and Butter, and a father and son named Fisher, were the victims. All of them, excepting young Fisher, leave widows and families. It is not clearly known as yet whether any persons were injured. The scene when the bodies were brought out was a very painful ono, the distress of the relatives being heartrending to witness.

"THE CHURCH AND OUR LIBERTIES."

On Wednesday evening a lecture on the subject "The church and our liberties " was delivered by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, in the schoolroom, Museum-street, Warring- ton. The chair was occupied by Dr. White. There was not a large attendance. Mr. Carleton, in the course of his- lecture, said it always appeared to him that there was-a certain section of the community who took for granted that the church'S influence had necessarily always been opposed to and especially hostile to the liberties of the people. That, however, was really not the case as the facts of his- tory incontestably proved, and from the church's very nature it was not likely that it should be the enemy of free- dom. LiberW was one of its watchwords. The church In fact interposed the only possible check upon the un- just exercise of temporal power, and if it were to be got rid. of then they should lie helplessly at the feet of any tyrant who was able to successfully grasp at absolute power. The- church was an institution by means of which the moral and spiritual forces of the world were organised. She had at her command powers which were beyond the control of earthly sovereign. and her influence was .naturally dreaded by the social, and political tyrant in whatever form he pre- sented himself. As they might expect, history showed them the church sometimes in hostility with the sovereign, some-. times at variance with the aristocracy, and sometimes hav- ing to encounter the hostility of an unreasoning populace. He was aware that the church had not always truly conceived what her mission WV!, and had sought for her-- self the exercise of temporal power. But that was an evil that lay more at the door of the Church of Rome than at that of the English Church proper, and it was part of the corruption through which they had suffered in times past. But he thought that as a rule if there had been any cause of complaint in the past it had been that the temporal power had sought to encroach upon the ecclesiastical power,.aud that he considered was the great danger of the- present time. He thought they were now face to face with an intolerence as fierce and unreasoning as some of the worst specimens which our history furnished. The lecturer then referred to the actions of some of the early archbishops and bishops in resisting the tyrannay of the monarchs, and he also criticised the conduct of the Puritans. He re- marked that the Nonconformists had produced no literature of their own of real standard value, and whenever they entered upon a discussion they were bound to rely for their argu- ments upon works produced by churchmen. Dealing with the church's action in civil matters he said they should bear in mind that the progress of toleration had been made under-the auspices of the churcb. During the whole of the period the church had been in the ascendant. She was the church of the nation, and unless the ascendancy of the church had been on the whole favourable to the progress to which he had referred it certainly could not have taken place. With Parliament composedexclusively of churchmen, and with all the great organisations of the state in the hands of churchmen it was absurd to say that measures of toleration could have passed unless they commanded large bodies of the Churchmen of the time. (Applause.) He disputed the claims to credit in connection with progress of toleration which were put forward by Dissenters; and he thought if any credit for disinterested motives was to be awarded it ought to be to those who had given toleration, and ?lotto those on whom it bad been bestowed. They had in the growth and establishment of Dissent the remarkable fact forced upon them that Dissent had been estaislished by Act of Parliament. The various measures of toleration were really so many Acts assigning a status to the various bodies of Nonconformists. From history, Indeed, it appeared that the Dissenters had been a good deal more established by Act of Parliament than the Church of Englgnd had. Ref erring to the proposals to disendow the Church, he ad- vised the Dissenting bodies to wait until by the accumula. tion Qf the benevolences of their own children they had 1

FOTICE IS HICHEBY GIVEN that at a Spee'al Meeting of the Local Board for the district of Baydook, called in pursuance of the provisions of the Act 35 and :36 Victoria, cap. 91, and held on Wednesday, the 11th day of February, 1885, the following Resolution was passed by an absolute majority of the whole number of the said Local Board, that is to say : " RPsolved, that by an absolute majority of the whole num- ber of the Local Board for the district of Haydock, and present at this meeting, that, in the judgment of the said Local Bard assembled, being the governing body for the said dtstrict, it is expedient for such governing body to oppose a Bill in Parliament to be promoted in the next session called ' be St. Helens and Wigan Junctions Rail- way Bill, 1885; and that the said Local Board, as such govetning body of the said district, do opt:Apse the said Bill in Parliament, and for that purpose apply tile General Dis- trict Fund, and General District Rate, under the control of such governing body, or such portion thereof as May be necessary, for the payment of the costs and expenses attending the same." JOSEPH EVANS, Chairman of the raid Local Board. Dated this 12th day of February, ISM

THE EXCESSIVE MORTALITY IN ST. HELENS. From the annual report of the Registrar-General which Las recently been issued, it appears that during the quarter just ended there vies a considerable increase in the mortality of St. Helens. In September quarter there were 371 deaths, and the present -report gave 520, or 149 more, equd to an annual rate of 33 7 per 1,000 of the population—estimated to have been in middle of last teat 61,245, showing an in- crease. of 1,380 on the total of 1883. The rate was 125 more than that of the 50 great towns,in England and Wales, and was the greatest death \rate among the 70 great towns in England and Wales. It was chiefly owing to a most 'die- estrous epidemic of measles, which were fatal in as many as 135 cases. BIRTHS AND DEATHS iN THE DTSTRICT FOR THS PAST QUARTER.
